Lord’s Day 1: Our Only Comfort Introduction The catechism opens not with a definition or a demand but with a question every human heart asks sooner or later: what will hold me up when everything else gives way? Its answer is not an idea but a person. We belong to Jesus Christ, body and soul, in life and in death, and the whole catechism that follows simply unfolds what that belonging means: how badly we needed it, how Christ won it, and how a grateful life flows from it. What is thy only comfort in life and in death? That I, with body and soul, both in life and in death, am not my own, but belong to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ, who with his precious blood has fully satisfied for all my sins, and redeemed me from all the power of the devil; and so preserves me that without the will of my Father in heaven not a hair can fall from my head; yea, that all things must work together for my salvation. Wherefore, by his Holy Spirit, he also assures me of eternal life, and makes me heartily willing and ready henceforth to live unto him. My only comfort is that I am not my own. Body and soul, in life and in death, I belong to my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ. With his precious blood he has fully paid for all my sins and set me free from all the power of the devil. He watches over me so carefully that not a hair can fall from my head without the will of my Father in heaven; in fact, all things must work together for my salvation. And so, by his Holy Spirit, he also assures me of eternal life and makes me wholeheartedly willing and ready from now on to live for him. Most of us assume that freedom means belonging to ourselves, yet that is exactly what leaves us anxious, because everything then rests on us. The catechism’s first word of comfort is the opposite: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). We belong to someone who has already paid for every sin, who keeps us in his Father’s hand (John 10:28–29), and who promises that all things work for our good (Romans 8:28). Notice that obedience comes last, and comes as a gift: the Spirit makes us willing to live for the one who first lived and died for us. 1 Corinthians 6:19–20; Romans 14:7–9 1 Corinthians 3:23; Titus 2:14 1 Peter 1:18–19; 1 John 1:7; 2:2 John 8:34–36; Hebrews 2:14–15; 1 John 3:8 John 6:39–40; 10:27–30; Matthew 10:29–31 Romans 8:28 2 Corinthians 1:21–22; Ephesians 1:13–14; Romans 8:15–16 Romans 8:14 How many things are necessary for thee to know, that thou in this comfort mayest live and die happily? Three things: First, the greatness of my sin and misery. Second, how I am redeemed from all my sins and misery. Third, how I am to be thankful to God for such redemption. Three things. First, how great my sin and misery are. Second, how I am set free from all my sins and misery. Third, how I am to thank God for such deliverance. This short answer gives the shape of the whole catechism, and of the Christian life: guilt, grace and gratitude. We cannot treasure a rescue until we see the danger we were in, and we will not live gratefully until we see how freely we were rescued (Luke 7:47). The order matters: thankfulness is not the price we pay to be saved but the natural response of people who have been (Ephesians 2:8–10). Romans 3:9–10; 1 John 1:10 John 17:3; Acts 4:12; 10:43 Matthew 5:16; Romans 6:13; Ephesians 5:8–10; 1 Peter 2:9–10

Lord’s Day 2: Knowing Our Misery Part 1: Our Misery Before the catechism speaks of rescue it holds up a mirror. The law of God, summed up by Jesus as love for God and neighbour, shows us not only what we ought to be but what we are. This is the hardest part of the catechism to read, and it is meant to be: the bad news is told so that the good news can be heard as good. Whence knowest thou thy misery? Out of the Law of God. From the law of God. We usually measure ourselves against other people, and by that standard most of us come off reasonably well. God’s law measures us against his own goodness, and there the comparison collapses: “through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20). Yet this is a kindness. A doctor who tells us the truth about our illness is far more loving than one who hides it, because only then will we go to the cure. Romans 3:20; 7:7–25 What does the Law of God require of us? This Christ teaches us in sum, Matt 22: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength. This is the first and great commandment; and the second is like unto it: Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.—On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. Christ teaches us this in summary in Matthew 22: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind and with all your strength. This is the first and great commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets. God’s law is not first a list of rules but a call to love: whole-hearted love for God and self-giving love for others (Matthew 22:37–40). That makes it more searching, not less. We can keep rules while our hearts are cold, but no one can pretend to have loved God with all their heart and their neighbour as themselves every day of their life. Only one person ever has, and he kept this law for us. Deuteronomy 6:5; Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 22:37–40; Mark 12:30–31; Luke 10:27 Canst thou keep all this perfectly? No; for I am by nature prone to hate God and my neighbor. No. By nature I am inclined to hate God and my neighbour. This sounds harsh until we notice how naturally we resent being told what to do, how readily we put ourselves first, and how often love for others turns out to be love for ourselves in disguise. Scripture says the mind set on the flesh is hostile to God (Romans 8:7). The catechism is honest about this not to crush us but to free us from the exhausting pretence that we are better than we are, so that we can be loved as we really are. Romans 3:9–20, 23; 1 John 1:8, 10 Genesis 6:5; Jeremiah 17:9; Romans 7:23–24; 8:7; Ephesians 2:1–3; Titus 3:3

Lord’s Day 3: Created Good, Fallen Deep Part 1: Our Misery If we are so bent towards evil, did God make us this way? The catechism answers firmly: no. We were made good, in God’s own image, for joy in knowing him. Our misery is not our original design but a ruin we brought on ourselves, and the only remedy deep enough is to be born again by the Spirit of God. Did God create man thus wicked and perverse? No; but God created man good, and after his own image—that is, in righteousness and true holiness; that he might rightly know God his Creator, heartily love him, and live with him in eternal blessedness, to praise and glorify him. No. God created human beings good and in his own image, that is, in true righteousness and holiness, so that they might rightly know God their Creator, love him with all their heart, and live with him in eternal happiness, to praise and glorify him. The Bible’s story does not begin with sin but with goodness: “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). We were made to know God, love him and enjoy him for ever, which is why nothing smaller ever fully satisfies us. Our misery is the misery of royalty in exile, and the gospel is the news that the image we defaced is being restored in Christ (Colossians 3:10). Genesis 1:31 Genesis 1:26–27 Ephesians 4:24; Colossians 3:10 Psalm 8 Whence, then, comes this depraved nature of man? From the fall and disobedience of our first parents, Adam and Eve, in Paradise, whereby our nature became so corrupt that we are all conceived and born in sin. From the fall and disobedience of our first parents, Adam and Eve, in Paradise. Because of it our nature became so corrupt that we are all conceived and born in sin. Sin is not only something we do; it is something we inherit, a twist in our nature that we did not choose and cannot undo (Psalm 51:5). That is humbling, but it also explains a great deal about the world and about our own hearts. And it sets up the gospel’s great answer: as one man’s disobedience brought ruin to many, so one man’s obedience brings righteousness to many (Romans 5:18–19). Genesis 3 Romans 5:12, 18–19 Psalm 51:5; John 3:6 But are we so far depraved that we are wholly unapt to any good, and prone to all evil? Yes; unless we are born again by the Spirit of God. Yes, we are so corrupt that we are wholly unable to do any good and inclined to all evil, unless we are born again by the Spirit of God. This does not mean we are as bad as we could possibly be, or that unbelievers never do kind things. It means that sin has reached every part of us, so that nothing we do comes from a heart that truly loves God above all, and we cannot change that heart ourselves. That is why Jesus said, “You must be born again” (John 3:7). The good news is that what we cannot do, the Spirit can and does. Genesis 6:5; 8:21; Job 14:4; Isaiah 53:6 John 3:3–5

Lord’s Day 4: God’s Justice and Our Guilt Part 1: Our Misery Three honest objections are raised and answered. Is God unfair to demand what we cannot do? Will he really punish sin? Is he not merciful? The catechism does not soften the answers, because only when we see that God is truly just can we see how astonishing it is that he is also the one who justifies. Does not God, then, wrong man by requiring of him in his law that which he can not perform? No; for God so made man that he could perform it; but man, through the instigation of the devil, by willful disobedience deprived himself and all his posterity of this power. No. God created human beings able to keep it. But at the devil’s prompting, by deliberate disobedience, they robbed themselves and all their descendants of this ability. If someone borrows a fortune and squanders it, the lender does not wrong him by asking for it back. Our inability to keep God’s law is not an innocent weakness but the result of turning away from him (Ecclesiastes 7:29). Yet the catechism is not building a case against us for its own sake: it is clearing the ground so that we stop making excuses and run to the only one who can pay what we owe. Genesis 1:31; Ephesians 4:24 Genesis 3:13; John 8:44 Genesis 3:6; Romans 5:12, 18–19 Will God suffer such disobedience and apostasy to go unpunished? By no means; but he is terribly displeased with our inborn as well as actual sins, and will punish them in just judgment in time and eternity, as he has declared: Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law, to do them. Certainly not. He is terribly angry with the sin we are born with as well as the sins we commit, and he will punish them by a just judgment both now and for ever, as he has declared: Cursed is everyone who does not keep on doing everything written in the book of the law. We often think a loving God would overlook sin, but we would never say that of a loving parent watching their child being harmed. God’s anger is not a temper but the settled opposition of perfect love to everything that destroys what he loves. The verse the catechism quotes (Galatians 3:10) is the very curse that Paul goes on to say Christ became for us (Galatians 3:13). Exodus 34:7; Psalm 5:4–6; Nahum 1:2; Romans 1:18; Ephesians 5:6; Hebrews 9:27 Galatians 3:10; Deuteronomy 27:26 Is, then, God not also merciful? God is indeed merciful, but he is likewise just; wherefore his justice requires that sin, which is committed against the most high majesty of God, be also punished with extreme, that is, with everlasting punishment both of body and soul. God is certainly merciful, but he is also just. His justice requires that sin, committed against the supreme majesty of God, be punished with the supreme penalty, that is, with eternal punishment of body and soul. The catechism refuses to set God’s mercy against his justice, as though one had to give way to the other. At the cross they meet: God is both “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). If God simply ignored evil he would not be good, and if he simply punished it we would have no hope. In Christ he does neither, and both. Exodus 34:6–7; Psalm 103:8–9 Exodus 34:7; Deuteronomy 7:9–11; Psalm 5:4–6; Hebrews 10:30–31 Matthew 25:35–46

Lord’s Day 5: The Need for a Mediator Part 2: Our Deliverance Here the catechism turns to our deliverance, and it begins by reasoning. If God’s justice must be satisfied, who can do it? Not we ourselves, who only add to the debt, and not any mere creature. What we need is someone who is truly human, without sin, and yet more powerful than any creature: someone who is God himself. Since, then, by the righteous judgment of God we deserve temporal and eternal punishment, what is required that we may escape this punishment and be again received into favor? God wills that his justice be satisfied; therefore must we make full satisfaction to the same, either by ourselves or by another. God requires that his justice be satisfied. So full payment must be made, either by ourselves or by another. Forgiveness is never free for the one who forgives: someone always absorbs the cost. The catechism takes seriously that sin is a real debt, not a misunderstanding. The wonder of the gospel is not that God waives the debt but that he himself pays it (Romans 8:3–4). Exodus 23:7; Romans 2:1–11 Isaiah 53:11; Romans 8:3–4 Can we ourselves make this satisfaction? By no means; on the contrary, we daily increase our guilt. Certainly not. On the contrary, we increase our debt every day. Most religions and most of our private hopes rest on the idea that we can make up for what we have done wrong. The catechism gently closes that door, not to shut us out but to point us to the only door that is open. Every attempt to pay our own way only adds to the account (Matthew 6:12; Romans 2:4–5). Matthew 6:12; Romans 2:4–5 Can any mere creature make satisfaction for us? None; for, first, God will not punish, in any other creature, that of which man has made himself guilty; and, further, no mere creature can sustain the burden of God’s eternal wrath against sin, and redeem others therefrom. No. First, God will not punish another creature for the sin a human being has committed. Further, no mere creature can bear the weight of God’s eternal anger against sin and set others free from it. The Old Testament sacrifices could never take away sins (Hebrews 10:4); they pointed forward to one who could. Our rescuer had to be one of us, because it is human sin that must be answered for (Hebrews 2:14–18). And he had to be more than one of us, because no creature could carry the full weight of that answer and live. Ezekiel 18:4, 20; Hebrews 2:14–18 Psalm 49:7–9; 130:3; Hebrews 10:4 What manner of mediator and redeemer, then, must we seek? One who is a true and sinless man, and yet more powerful than all creatures; that is, one who is at the same time true God. One who is a true and righteous human being, and yet more powerful than all creatures; that is, one who is also true God. Step by step the catechism has described a person no one could have invented: fully human, sinless, and fully divine. Then, in the next Lord’s Day, it names him. The gospel is not a theory we reasoned our way to but a person God gave (1 Timothy 2:5; Isaiah 9:6). Romans 1:3; 1 Corinthians 15:21; Hebrews 2:17 Isaiah 53:9; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 7:26 Isaiah 7:14; 9:6; Jeremiah 23:6; John 1:1

Lord’s Day 6: True God and True Man Part 2: Our Deliverance Why must the mediator be both human and divine, and who is he? The catechism answers with the heart of the Christian faith: Jesus Christ, God become man, freely given to us. And it traces the gospel back to the first promise in the garden, foreshadowed through all the sacrifices of Israel and fulfilled in the Son. Why must he be a true and sinless man? Because the justice of God requires that the same human nature which has sinned should make satisfaction for sin; but no man, being himself a sinner, could satisfy for others. Because God’s justice requires that the same human nature that has sinned should pay for sin, and no one who is himself a sinner could pay for others. Christ did not rescue us from a distance. He took our nature, lived our life and died our death, so that the one who stood in our place was truly one of us (Hebrews 2:14–17). And because he had no sin of his own to answer for, his death could count for others (1 Peter 3:18). Romans 5:12, 15; 1 Corinthians 15:21; Hebrews 2:14–16 Hebrews 7:26–27; 1 Peter 3:18 Why must he be at the same time true God? That by the power of his Godhead he might bear, in his manhood, the burden of God’s wrath, and so obtain for and restore to us righteousness and life. So that by the power of his divine nature he might bear the weight of God’s anger in his human nature, and so win for us and restore to us righteousness and life. Only God could carry what had to be carried. The cross is not a third party being punished by an angry God, but God himself, in the person of his Son, bearing the cost of our sin (2 Corinthians 5:19). That is why the gift of righteousness and life is so secure: it was won by one who could not fail (Isaiah 53:4–5). Isaiah 9:5; 53:4–5 John 3:16; 2 Corinthians 5:21 But who, now, is that mediator, who is at the same time true God and a true, sinless man? Our Lord Jesus Christ, who is freely given unto us for complete redemption and righteousness. Our Lord Jesus Christ, who was freely given to us for our complete deliverance and righteousness. After all the careful reasoning, the answer is a name. Everything we need, wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption, is found in one person who was given to us as a gift (1 Corinthians 1:30). Christianity is not first a set of instructions but an introduction: here is the one who saves. Matthew 1:21–23; Luke 2:11; 1 Timothy 2:5; 3:16 1 Corinthians 1:30 Whence knowest thou this? From the Holy Gospel, which God himself first revealed in Paradise, afterwards proclaimed by the holy Patriarchs and Prophets, and foreshadowed by the sacrifices and other ceremonies of the law, and finally fulfilled by his well-beloved Son. From the holy gospel. God himself first revealed it in Paradise; later he proclaimed it through the holy patriarchs and prophets and portrayed it through the sacrifices and other ceremonies of the law; and finally he fulfilled it through his own dearly loved Son. The Bible is one story with one hero. The promise that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15) runs like a thread through Abraham, Moses, the sacrifices and the prophets until it is fulfilled in Jesus. As he himself showed on the road to Emmaus, all the Scriptures speak of him (Luke 24:27). Genesis 3:15 Genesis 22:18; 49:10 Isaiah 53; Jeremiah 23:5–6; Micah 7:18–20; Acts 10:43; Hebrews 1:1–2 Leviticus 1–7; John 5:46; Hebrews 10:1–10 Romans 10:4; Galatians 4:4–5; Colossians 2:17

Lord’s Day 7: True Faith Part 2: Our Deliverance How do we come to share in Christ? Not automatically, as we all shared in Adam, but by being joined to him through true faith. The catechism defines that faith beautifully, as both knowledge and wholehearted trust, and then introduces the Apostles’ Creed as a summary of what faith believes. Are all men, then, saved by Christ, as they have perished by Adam? No; only such as by true faith are ingrafted into him, and receive all his benefits. No. Only those who by true faith are grafted into him and accept all his benefits. Christ’s rescue is offered freely to all, but it is received by faith, the way a branch receives life by being grafted into the vine (John 15:5). Faith is not the thing that saves; Christ is. Faith is simply the empty hand that receives him (John 1:12). Matthew 7:14; 22:14 John 1:12; 3:16, 18, 36; Romans 11:16–21 What is true faith? It is not only a certain knowledge whereby I hold for truth all that God has revealed to us in his Word, but also a hearty trust which the Holy Ghost works in me by the Gospel, that not only to others, but to me also, forgiveness of sins, everlasting righteousness and salvation, are freely given by God, merely of grace, only for the sake of Christ’s merits. True faith is not only a sure knowledge by which I accept as true all that God has revealed to us in his Word. It is also a wholehearted trust, which the Holy Spirit creates in me through the gospel, that not only to others but also to me, God has freely given forgiveness of sins, everlasting righteousness and salvation, out of sheer grace, only because of what Christ has done. Faith has a head and a heart. It knows what God has said, but it also rests the whole weight of life on it, the way you trust a bridge not by admiring it but by walking across it (Hebrews 11:1). The most precious words here are “to me also”: the gospel is not just true in general but true for me, and the Spirit gives that personal confidence (Galatians 2:20). John 17:3, 17; Hebrews 11:1–3; James 2:19 Romans 4:18–21; 5:1; 10:10; Hebrews 4:14–16 Matthew 16:15–17; John 3:5; Acts 16:14 Romans 1:16; 10:17; 1 Corinthians 1:21 Romans 3:21–26; Galatians 2:16; Ephesians 2:8–10 Galatians 2:20 What is it, then, necessary for a Christian to believe? All that is promised us in the Gospel, which the articles of our catholic, undoubted Christian faith teach us in sum. Everything promised to us in the gospel, which the articles of our universal and undoubted Christian faith teach us in summary. Faith is not a vague feeling but trust in definite promises. The catechism points us to the Apostles’ Creed because it is the shared confession of Christians in every age and place (Jude 3). To believe the gospel is to join a great company that stretches back to the apostles themselves. Matthew 28:18–20; John 20:30–31 What are these Articles? I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth. And in Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, our Lord: who was conceived by the Holy Ghost, born of the Virgin Mary; suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, dead, and buried; he descended into Hades; the third day he rose from the dead; he ascended into Heaven, and sitteth at the right hand of God the Father Almighty; from, thence he shall come to judge the quick and the dead. I believe in the Holy Ghost; the holy Catholic Church; the communion of saints; the forgiveness of sins; the resurrection of the body, and the life everlasting. I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth. And in Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried. He descended into hell. On the third day he rose again from the dead. He ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit; the holy catholic church; the communion of saints; the forgiveness of sins; the resurrection of the body; and the life everlasting. The Creed is the gospel in a nutshell: who God is and what he has done. Almost every line is about events, not ideas, because Christianity is news about what God has done in history. The word “catholic” here means universal: the one church of Christ throughout the world and through all ages, not any single denomination. 1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 1 Timothy 3:16

Lord’s Day 8: One God in Three Persons Part 2: Our Deliverance The Creed has three parts because God is three persons: the Father who made us, the Son who redeemed us and the Spirit who makes us holy. The catechism does not try to explain the Trinity away. It simply confesses what God has shown of himself: one true and eternal God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. How are these Articles divided? Into three parts: The first is of God the Father and our creation; the second, of God the Son and our redemption; the third, of God the Holy Ghost and our sanctification. Into three parts: the first is about God the Father and our creation; the second about God the Son and our redemption; the third about God the Holy Spirit and our sanctification. The Christian life is lived in the embrace of all three persons of God. The Father made us and keeps us, the Son bought us back, and the Spirit makes us new (1 Peter 1:2). Every blessing comes from the Father, through the Son, by the Spirit, and that is why the Creed and the Christian life alike are shaped like the Trinity. 1 Peter 1:1–2; 2 Corinthians 13:14 Since there is but one Divine Being, why speakest thou of three, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost? Because God has so revealed himself in his Word that these three distinct Persons are the one, true, eternal God. Because that is how God has revealed himself in his Word: these three distinct persons are the one, true, eternal God. We do not believe in the Trinity because we have solved it but because God has revealed it, most of all in Jesus, who prayed to his Father and promised the Spirit (John 14:16–17). At the heart of reality, then, is not a lonely power but a communion of love, and the gospel invites us into it. At Jesus’ baptism the Father speaks, the Son is baptised and the Spirit descends (Matthew 3:16–17). Deuteronomy 6:4; 1 Corinthians 8:4, 6 Isaiah 61:1; Matthew 3:16–17; 28:18–19; Luke 4:18; Titus 3:4–6

Lord’s Day 9: God the Father and Creator Part 2: Our Deliverance The first article of the Creed could be read as a cold statement about a distant Maker. The catechism makes it intensely personal: the almighty Creator of everything is, for Christ’s sake, my God and my Father, able and willing to care for me. That changes how we face every day, including the hard ones. What dost thou believe when thou sayest: I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of Heaven and Earth? That the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who of nothing made heaven and earth, with all that in them is, who likewise upholds and governs the same by his eternal counsel and providence, is for the sake of Christ his Son my God and my Father, in whom I so trust as to have no doubt that he will provide me with all things necessary for body and soul; and further, that whatever evil he sends upon me in this vale of tears, he will turn to my good; for he is able to do it, being Almighty God, and willing also, being a faithful Father. That the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who out of nothing created heaven and earth and everything in them, and who still upholds and rules them by his eternal counsel and providence, is my God and my Father for the sake of Christ his Son. I trust him so completely that I have no doubt he will provide whatever I need for body and soul, and that he will turn to my good whatever evil he sends me in this sad world. He is able to do this, because he is almighty God; and he wants to do it, because he is a faithful Father. Many people believe in a Creator; far fewer dare to call him Father. The catechism grounds that confidence not in our worthiness but in Christ: because the Son is ours, his Father is ours too (John 20:17). Here are the two things we most need to know about anyone we depend on, that they can help and that they want to. In God both are perfect, so even sorrow in this “vale of tears” is held by a Father who means it for our good (Romans 8:28). Genesis 1–2; Exodus 20:11; Psalm 33:6; Isaiah 44:24; Acts 4:24; 14:15 Psalm 104; Matthew 6:30; 10:29; Ephesians 1:11 John 1:12–13; Romans 8:15–16; Galatians 4:4–7; Ephesians 1:5 Psalm 55:22; Matthew 6:25–26; Luke 12:22–31 Romans 8:28 Genesis 18:14; Romans 8:31–39 Matthew 7:9–11

Lord’s Day 10: The Providence of God Part 2: Our Deliverance Providence is the catechism’s word for God’s ongoing care of everything he has made. Nothing happens by chance; all things come from our Father’s hand. That truth is not given to satisfy curiosity but to give us patience in trouble, thankfulness in good times and a quiet confidence about the future. What dost thou understand by the Providence of God? The almighty and every where present power of God, whereby, as it were by his hand, he still upholds heaven and earth, with all creatures, and so governs them that herbs and grass, rain and drought, fruitful and barren years, meat and drink, health and sickness, riches and poverty, yea, all things, come not by chance, but by his fatherly hand. The almighty and ever-present power of God by which, as with his own hand, he still upholds heaven and earth and all creatures, and so rules them that leaf and blade, rain and drought, fruitful and barren years, food and drink, health and sickness, riches and poverty, indeed all things, come to us not by chance but from his fatherly hand. Nothing in our lives is random, and nothing is outside the reach of our Father’s care (Matthew 10:29–30). This does not make suffering easy to understand, but it means suffering is never meaningless. The same hand that sends rain and drought was pierced for us, so we can trust it even when we cannot trace it. Jeremiah 23:23–24; Acts 17:24–28 Hebrews 1:3 Jeremiah 5:24; Acts 14:15–17; John 9:3; Proverbs 22:2 Proverbs 16:33 Matthew 10:29 What does it profit us to know that God has created, and by his providence still upholds all things? That we may be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity, and for what is future have good confidence in our faithful God and Father that no creature shall separate us from his love, since all creatures are so in his hand that without his will they can not so much as move. That we can be patient when things go against us, thankful when things go well, and, for the future, have firm confidence in our faithful God and Father that nothing will separate us from his love, since all creatures are so completely in his hand that without his will they cannot even move. Belief in God’s providence is meant to shape how we feel, not just what we think. It steadies us in hard times, humbles us in good times, and frees us from fear of the future, because nothing in all creation “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). The question is not whether life will be hard, but whose hands it is in. Job 1:21–22; James 1:3 Deuteronomy 8:10; 1 Thessalonians 5:18 Psalm 55:22; Romans 5:3–5; 8:38–39 Job 1:12; 2:6; Proverbs 21:1; Acts 17:24–28

Lord’s Day 11: The Name Jesus Part 2: Our Deliverance With the second article the catechism turns to the Son, starting with his names. Jesus means Saviour, and he is not one helper among many but the only and complete Saviour. To look anywhere else, to saints, to ourselves or to anything we can do, is in effect to deny him. Why is the Son of God called Jesus, that is, Saviour? Because he saves us from our sins; and no salvation is to be either sought or found in any other. Because he saves us from our sins, and because salvation is not to be looked for, or found, in anyone else. The angel told Joseph to call him Jesus, “for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). His very name is a promise. And because there is “no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12), we are freed from the endless search for something else to rescue us. Matthew 1:21; Hebrews 7:25 Isaiah 43:11; John 15:4–5; Acts 4:11–12; 1 Timothy 2:5 Do such, then, believe in the only Saviour Jesus who seek their salvation and welfare of saints, of themselves, or any where else? No; although they may make their boast of him, yet in act they deny the only Saviour Jesus. For either Jesus is not a complete Saviour, or they who by true faith receive this Saviour must have in him all that is necessary to their salvation. No. Although they boast of him in words, they deny the only Saviour Jesus by what they do. For either Jesus is not a complete Saviour, or those who by true faith receive this Saviour must find in him all they need for their salvation. This is one of the most freeing answers in the catechism. It is very easy to trust Jesus and something else alongside him: our good record, our religious performance, the prayers of the saints. But a half-Saviour is no Saviour. In Christ we have been “filled” (Colossians 2:10), so we do not need to add anything, and we must not. 1 Corinthians 1:12–13; Galatians 5:4 Colossians 1:19–20; 2:10; 1 John 1:7

Lord’s Day 12: Christ, the Anointed One Part 2: Our Deliverance Christ is not a surname but a title: the Anointed One. In Israel, prophets, priests and kings were anointed. Jesus is all three at once, and the catechism adds a lovely turn: by faith we share his anointing, so every Christian is in a small way a prophet, priest and king. Why is he called Christ, that is, Anointed? Because he is ordained of God the Father, and anointed with the Holy Ghost, to be our chief Prophet and Teacher, who fully reveals to us the secret counsel and will of God concerning our redemption; and our only High Priest, who by the one sacrifice of his body has redeemed us, and ever liveth to make intercession for us with the Father; and our eternal King, who governs us by his Word and Spirit, and defends and preserves us in the redemption obtained for us. Because he has been appointed by God the Father and anointed with the Holy Spirit to be our chief prophet and teacher, who fully reveals to us the secret counsel and will of God for our deliverance; our only high priest, who has set us free by the one sacrifice of his body and always pleads for us with the Father; and our eternal king, who rules us by his Word and Spirit, and who guards and keeps us in the freedom he has won for us. We need all three. We need a prophet because we are ignorant of God, a priest because we are guilty before God, and a king because we are weak and surrounded by enemies. Jesus is each of these perfectly: he speaks the truth, he offered himself once for all and still prays for us (Hebrews 7:25), and he rules us with a love that will never let us go. Psalm 45:7; Isaiah 61:1; Luke 3:21–22; 4:14–19; Hebrews 1:9 Deuteronomy 18:15; Acts 3:22 John 1:18; 15:15 Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7:17 Hebrews 9:12; 10:11–14 Romans 8:34; Hebrews 9:24 Matthew 21:5; Zechariah 9:9 Matthew 28:18–20; John 10:28; Revelation 12:10–11 But why art thou called a Christian? Because by faith I am a member of Christ, and thus a partaker of his anointing; in order that I also may confess his name, may present myself a living sacrifice of thankfulness to him, and may with free conscience fight against sin and the devil in this life, and hereafter, in eternity, reign with him over all creatures. Because by faith I am a member of Christ and so I share in his anointing. I am anointed to confess his name, to present myself to him as a living sacrifice of thanks, to fight with a free conscience against sin and the devil in this life, and afterwards to reign with him for ever over all creation. To be a Christian is to be joined to Christ, and so to share what he is. Every believer, not just ministers, is called to speak of him, to offer their life to God in gratitude (Romans 12:1) and to resist evil with a clear conscience. The church is “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), and the destiny of the humblest believer is to reign with Christ. 1 Corinthians 12:12–27 Acts 2:17; 1 John 2:27 Matthew 10:32; Romans 10:9–10; Hebrews 13:15 Romans 12:1; 1 Peter 2:5, 9 Galatians 5:16–17; Ephesians 6:11; 1 Timothy 1:18–19 Matthew 25:34; 2 Timothy 2:12

Lord’s Day 13: God’s Only Son, Our Lord Part 2: Our Deliverance Christ is God’s Son by nature; we become God’s children by adoption, by grace, for his sake. And he is our Lord, not by force but by purchase, because he bought us with his own blood. Both titles turn out to be full of comfort. Why is he called God’s only-begotten Son, since we also are the children of God? Because Christ alone is the eternal natural Son of God; but we are children of God by adoption through grace for his sake. Because Christ alone is the eternal, natural Son of God. We, however, are children of God by adoption, through grace, for his sake. Jesus has always been the Son; we are welcomed into the family. Adoption is one of the most tender pictures in Scripture: we are not servants hoping to earn a place but children who already have one, and who can cry “Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15). All of it is “for his sake”, so it is as secure as Christ’s own place in the Father’s love. John 1:1–3, 14, 18; Hebrews 1 John 1:12; Romans 8:14–17; Ephesians 1:5–6 Why callest thou him our Lord? Because, not with silver or gold, but with his precious blood, he has redeemed and purchased us, body and soul, from sin and from all the power of the devil, to be his own. Because he has set us free and bought us, body and soul, from sin and from all the power of the devil, not with gold or silver but with his precious blood, to be his very own. Most lords rule by power and take what they want. Jesus is Lord by having given everything. He bought us “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). To call him Lord, then, is not to submit to a tyrant but to come home to the one who loved us enough to pay for us. 1 Peter 1:18–19 Colossians 1:13–14; Hebrews 2:14–15 1 Corinthians 6:20; 1 Timothy 2:5–6

Lord’s Day 14: Conceived and Born Part 2: Our Deliverance The eternal Son of God became truly human, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. He did not stop being God; he took our flesh. And his holy conception and birth do something for us: his purity covers the sin with which we were born. What is the meaning of Conceived by the Holy Ghost, born of the Virgin Mary? That the eternal Son of God, who is and continues true and eternal God, took upon him the very nature of man, of the flesh and blood of the Virgin Mary, by the operation of the Holy Ghost, so that he also might be the true seed of David, like unto his brethren in all things, sin excepted. That the eternal Son of God, who is and remains true and eternal God, took on a true human nature from the flesh and blood of the Virgin Mary, through the work of the Holy Spirit. So he also became the true descendant of David, like his brothers in every way except for sin. The Christmas story is not a myth but the moment God came near. The Son did not lay aside his divinity, but took on our full humanity (John 1:14), so that he could be our brother as well as our Lord. He knows from the inside what it is to be weak, tired and tempted, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). John 1:1; 10:30–36; Romans 1:3; 9:5; Colossians 1:15–17; 1 John 5:20 Luke 1:35 Matthew 1:18–23; John 1:14; Galatians 4:4; Hebrews 2:14 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 132:11; Matthew 1:1; Romans 1:3 Philippians 2:7; Hebrews 2:17 Hebrews 4:15; 7:26–27 What benefit dost thou receive from the holy conception and birth of Christ? That he is our Mediator, and with his innocence and perfect holiness covers, in the sight of God, my sin wherein I was conceived. That he is our mediator, and that with his innocence and perfect holiness he covers, in God’s sight, the sin in which I was conceived. Christ’s holiness reaches back to the very beginning of our lives. Our sin is not only in what we have done but in what we were from the start (Psalm 51:5). But his life was holy from its first moment, and that perfect life covers ours. There is no part of our story too early or too deep for his grace to reach. 1 Timothy 2:5–6; Hebrews 9:13–15 Romans 8:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 4:4–5; 1 Peter 1:18–19

Lord’s Day 15: He Suffered Part 2: Our Deliverance The Creed leaps from Christ’s birth to his suffering, and the catechism explains why. His whole life, and above all its end, was a bearing of God’s anger against sin in our place. He was condemned by an earthly judge so that we might be acquitted by the heavenly one, and he died the cursed death of the cross to take our curse away. What dost thou understand by the word Suffered? That all the time he lived on earth, but especially at the end of his life, he bore, in body and soul, the wrath of God against the sin of the whole human race, in order that by his passion, as the only atoning sacrifice, he might redeem our body and soul from everlasting damnation, and obtain for us the grace of God, righteousness, and eternal life. That all through his life on earth, but especially at the end of it, he bore in body and soul the anger of God against the sin of the whole human race. He did this so that by his suffering, as the only atoning sacrifice, he might set us free, body and soul, from eternal condemnation, and win for us God’s grace, righteousness and eternal life. Jesus’ suffering did not begin at Gethsemane. He was born in poverty, rejected by his own and misunderstood by his friends; he was “a man of sorrows” (Isaiah 53:3). On the cross that suffering reached its depth, as he bore what we deserved. Whatever we suffer, we never suffer the anger of God, because he has already borne it for us. Isaiah 53; 1 Peter 2:24; 3:18 Romans 3:25; Hebrews 10:14; 1 John 2:2; 4:10 Romans 8:1–4; Galatians 3:13 John 3:16; Romans 3:24–26 Why did he suffer under Pontius Pilate, as judge? That he, being innocent, might be condemned by the temporal judge, and thereby deliver us from the severe judgment of God to which we were exposed. So that he, though innocent, might be condemned by an earthly judge, and in that way set us free from the severe judgment of God that was to fall on us. Pilate found no guilt in him and still condemned him (Luke 23:13–24). That injustice was the very means of our justice. The innocent was declared guilty so that the guilty could be declared innocent: “He was pierced for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5). Luke 23:13–24; John 19:4, 12–16 Isaiah 53:4–5; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13 Is there any thing more in his having been crucified than if he had died some other death? Yes; for thereby I am assured that he took on himself the curse which lay upon me, because the death of the cross was accursed of God. Yes. Because of it I am sure that he took on himself the curse that lay on me, since death on a cross was cursed by God. The law said that anyone hanged on a tree was under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23). Jesus chose that death deliberately. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The cross is the place where the worst thing that could happen to us happened to him instead. Galatians 3:10–13 Deuteronomy 21:23

Lord’s Day 16: Dead, Buried, Descended Part 2: Our Deliverance Christ really died and was really buried. His death was the only possible payment for our sin, and because of it our own death is transformed: no longer a punishment but a doorway. This Lord’s Day also explains the line he descended into hell as Christ’s inner anguish on our behalf. Why was it necessary for Christ to suffer death? Because, by reason of the justice and truth of God, satisfaction for our sins could be made no other wise than by the death of the Son of God. Because, on account of God’s justice and truth, payment for our sins could not be made in any other way than by the death of the Son of God. If there had been an easier way, a loving Father would surely have taken it. Jesus prayed in Gethsemane that the cup might pass, and it did not (Matthew 26:39). The cross shows both how serious sin is and how great God’s love is: “the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23), and the Son paid them. Genesis 2:17 Romans 8:3–4; Philippians 2:8; Hebrews 2:9 Why was he buried? To show thereby that he was really dead. To show that he had really died. The burial is a quiet detail with a large point: Jesus did not faint or seem to die; he truly died and was laid in a tomb (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). That makes the resurrection what it is. And it means even the grave, the place we most fear, has been occupied and sanctified by our Lord. Isaiah 53:9; John 19:38–42; Acts 13:29; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4 Since, then, Christ died for us, why must we also die? Our death is not a satisfaction for our sin, but only a dying to sins and entering into eternal life. Our death is not a payment for our sins. Rather, it puts an end to sinning and is our entry into eternal life. For the believer, death has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55). It is still an enemy and still grievous, but it can no longer punish us, because Christ has taken the punishment. Death becomes the moment we finally stop sinning and go to be with Christ, which is “far better” (Philippians 1:23). Psalm 49:7 John 5:24; Philippians 1:21–23; 1 Thessalonians 5:9–10 What further benefit do we receive from the sacrifice and death of Christ on the cross? That by his power our old man is with him crucified, slain, and buried; that so the evil lusts of the flesh may no more reign in us, but that we may offer ourselves unto him a sacrifice of thanksgiving. That by his power our old self is crucified, put to death and buried with him, so that the evil desires of the flesh may no longer rule us, but that we may offer ourselves to him as a sacrifice of thanks. The cross does not only forgive us; it changes us. United to Christ, we have died with him to sin’s rule (Romans 6:6), and the old life no longer has the last word. Holiness, then, is not a grim effort to earn God’s favour but the grateful life of people who have been set free. Romans 6:5–11; Colossians 2:11–12 Romans 6:12–14 Romans 12:1; Ephesians 5:1–2 Why is it added: He descended into Hades? That in my greatest temptations I may be assured that Christ, my Lord, by his inexpressible anguish, pains, and terrors which he suffered in his soul on the cross and before, has redeemed me from the anguish and torment of hell. To assure me in my times of deepest anxiety and temptation that Christ my Lord, by suffering unspeakable anguish, pain and terror in his soul on the cross and before it, has delivered me from the anguish and torment of hell. The catechism reads this line of the Creed not as a journey after death but as the hell Jesus endured on the cross, when he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). He went into the darkness of abandonment so that we never will. In our darkest hours we can know that Christ has been further down than we will ever go, and he did it for us. Psalm 18:5–6; 116:3; Matthew 26:36–46; 27:45–46; Luke 22:44; Hebrews 5:7–10 Isaiah 53

Lord’s Day 17: He Rose Again Part 2: Our Deliverance The resurrection is not just a happy ending to the story of the cross. It is God’s seal that the payment was accepted. The catechism draws out three gifts: Christ’s victory makes his righteousness ours, his power raises us to a new life now, and his rising is the guarantee of our own. What benefit do we receive from the resurrection of Christ? First, by his resurrection he has overcome death, that he might make us partakers of the righteousness which by his death he has obtained for us. Secondly, we also are now by his power raised up to a new life. Thirdly the resurrection of Christ is to us a sure pledge of our blessed resurrection. First, by his resurrection he has overcome death, so that he could make us share in the righteousness he won for us by his death. Second, by his power we too are already raised to a new life. Third, Christ’s resurrection is a sure pledge to us of our own glorious resurrection. Easter changes the past, the present and the future. Christ “raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25), so our forgiveness is sealed; we are raised with him to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:4); and he is the “firstfruits” of a harvest that will include us (1 Corinthians 15:20). Christian hope is not wishful thinking but confidence in an event. Romans 4:25; 1 Corinthians 15:16–20; 1 Peter 1:3–5 Romans 6:5–11; Ephesians 2:4–6; Colossians 3:1–4 Romans 8:11; 1 Corinthians 15:12–23; Philippians 3:20–21

Lord’s Day 18: He Ascended into Heaven Part 2: Our Deliverance Christ went up bodily into heaven and is there for us. Does that mean he has left us? The catechism answers carefully: in his human nature he is in heaven, but in his divinity, majesty, grace and Spirit he is never absent from us. And his ascension brings rich gifts: an advocate, our own flesh in heaven, and the Spirit. How dost thou understand the words, He ascended into Heaven? That Christ, in sight of his disciples, was taken up from the earth into heaven, and in our behalf there continues, until he shall come again to judge the living and the dead. That Christ, while his disciples watched, was taken up from the earth into heaven, and that he is there for our good until he comes again to judge the living and the dead. The ascension is not Jesus going away but Jesus going ahead, to the Father’s right hand on our behalf (Hebrews 9:24). The one who sits on the throne of the universe is still a man, still our brother, still for us. And the angels promised that this same Jesus will come back in the same way (Acts 1:11). Luke 24:50–51; Acts 1:9–11 Romans 8:34; Ephesians 4:8–10; Hebrews 7:23–25; 9:24 Acts 1:11 Is not, then, Christ with us even unto the end of the world, as he has promised? Christ is true Man and true God: according to his human nature, he is now not upon earth; but according to his Godhead, majesty, grace, and Spirit, he is at no time absent from us. Christ is true man and true God. In his human nature he is no longer on earth, but in his divinity, majesty, grace and Spirit he is never absent from us. Jesus promised, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20), and he keeps that promise. His body is in heaven, but he is with us by his Spirit, more closely than he was with the disciples in Galilee (John 16:7). No believer is ever alone. Acts 1:9–11; 3:19–21 Matthew 28:20; John 14:16–19; 16:13 But are not, in this way, the two natures in Christ separated from one another, if the Manhood be not wherever the Godhead is? By no means; for since the Godhead is incomprehensible and every where present, it must follow that it is indeed beyond the bounds of the Manhood which it has assumed, but is yet none the less in the same also, and remains personally united to it. Certainly not. Since his divinity is not limited and is present everywhere, it must follow that it is beyond the bounds of the human nature it has taken on, and yet it is none the less in that human nature and remains personally united to it. This careful answer guards a precious truth: the Son of God is one person, fully God and fully man, and the two natures are never confused or divided. His humanity is not swallowed up in his divinity, which is why he remains truly one of us. The God who fills heaven and earth (Jeremiah 23:24) has bound himself for ever to our flesh. Jeremiah 23:23–24; Acts 7:48–49 John 1:14; 3:13; Colossians 2:9 What benefit do we receive from Christ’s ascension into heaven? First, that he is our Advocate in the presence of his Father in heaven. Secondly, that we have our flesh in heaven, as a sure pledge that he, as the Head, will also take us, his members, up to himself. Thirdly, that he sends us his Spirit, as an earnest, by whose power we seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God, and not things on the earth. First, he is our advocate in heaven before his Father. Second, we have our own flesh in heaven as a sure pledge that Christ our head will also take us, his members, up to himself. Third, he sends us his Spirit as a guarantee, by whose power we seek the things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God, and not the things on earth. Because of the ascension, someone is speaking up for us in heaven at this moment (1 John 2:1). Our humanity has already arrived where we are going, like the first of a family to reach a new home. And the Spirit he sends turns our hearts upward, so that we “seek the things that are above, where Christ is” (Colossians 3:1). Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1 John 14:2; 17:24; Ephesians 2:4–6 John 14:16; 2 Corinthians 1:21–22; 5:5 Colossians 3:1–4

Lord’s Day 19: Seated and Coming Again Part 2: Our Deliverance Christ now reigns at God’s right hand as head of his church, through whom the Father rules everything. From there he pours out gifts and protects his people. And he will return as judge: the very one who stood trial in our place, which turns the last judgment from a terror into a comfort. Why is it added, And sitteth at the right hand of God? Because Christ ascended into heaven for this end, that he might there appear as Head of his Church, by whom the Father governs all things. Because Christ ascended into heaven to show himself there as head of his church, through whom the Father governs all things. The universe is not ruled by chance or by the powers that seem strong, but by Jesus, the one who loves the church enough to die for it (Ephesians 1:20–23). Everything is under his feet, and he is head over everything “to the church”, that is, for its good. That is a firm place to stand when the world feels out of control. Ephesians 1:20–23; Colossians 1:18 Matthew 28:18; John 5:22–23 What benefit do we receive from this glory of our Head, Christ? First, that by his Holy Spirit he sheds forth heavenly gifts in us, his members; then, that by his power he defends and preserves us against all enemies. First, through his Holy Spirit he pours out heavenly gifts on us, his members. Second, by his power he defends us and keeps us safe from all enemies. The reigning Christ is not idle. He gives gifts to his people so that they can serve one another (Ephesians 4:7–12), and he guards them so that none is lost (John 10:28). The church’s life and survival through the centuries are not human achievements but signs of its living head. Acts 2:33; Ephesians 4:7–12 Psalm 110:1–2; John 10:27–30; Revelation 19:11–16 What comfort is it to thee that Christ shall come again to judge the quick and the dead? That in all my sorrows and persecutions, with uplifted head, I look for the self-same One who has before offered himself for me to the judgment of God, and removed from me all curse, to come again as Judge from heaven; who shall cast all his and my enemies into everlasting condemnation, but shall take me, with all his chosen ones, to himself, into heavenly joy and glory. In all my sorrow and persecution I lift up my head and confidently wait for the very same person who before offered himself for me to God’s judgment, and who removed the whole curse from me, to come from heaven as judge. He will throw all his enemies and mine into everlasting condemnation, but he will take me and all his chosen ones to himself into heavenly joy and glory. For many, the thought of a final judgment brings dread. The catechism turns it into comfort, because the judge is the one who has already been judged for us. That is why the early church prayed “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20). Justice will finally be done for every wrong, and those who belong to Christ will be welcomed home. Luke 21:28; Romans 8:22–25; Philippians 3:20–21; Titus 2:13–14 Matthew 25:31–46; 2 Thessalonians 1:6–10

Lord’s Day 20: God the Holy Spirit Part 2: Our Deliverance The third article of the Creed concerns the Holy Spirit, and the catechism says two things about him. He is fully God, with the Father and the Son. And he is given to me personally: he joins me to Christ by faith, shares Christ’s benefits with me, comforts me and stays with me for ever. What dost thou believe concerning the Holy Ghost? First, that he is co-eternal God with the Father and the Son. Secondly, that he is also given unto me, makes me by a true faith partaker of Christ and all his benefits, comforts me, and shall abide with me forever. First, that he is true and eternal God together with the Father and the Son. Second, that he has been given to me personally, so that by true faith he makes me share in Christ and all his benefits, comforts me, and will remain with me for ever. The Spirit is not a force or a feeling but a person, and he is God. His great work is to bring us to Christ and Christ to us: everything Jesus won becomes ours through the Spirit’s work in our hearts (Ephesians 1:13–14). Jesus called him “another Helper, to be with you forever” (John 14:16), so the believer is never left to manage alone. Genesis 1:1–2; Matthew 28:19; Acts 5:3–4; 1 Corinthians 3:16 1 Corinthians 6:19; 2 Corinthians 1:21–22; Galatians 4:6 Galatians 3:14 John 15:26; Acts 9:31 John 14:16–17; 1 Peter 4:14

Lord’s Day 21: The Church, the Saints, Forgiveness Part 2: Our Deliverance Christ is not only saving individuals but gathering a people. The catechism sees the church as Christ’s own work across all of history, and every believer as a living member of it. Belonging to it means sharing in Christ’s treasures and sharing our gifts with one another. And at its heart is the forgiveness of sins, so full that God will no longer remember them. What dost thou believe concerning the Holy Catholic Church? That out of the whole human race, from the beginning to the end of the world, the Son of God, by his Spirit and Word, gathers, defends, and preserves for himself unto everlasting life, a chosen communion in the unity of the true faith; and that I am, and forever shall remain, a living member of the same. I believe that the Son of God, through his Spirit and Word, out of the whole human race, from the beginning of the world to its end, gathers, protects and keeps for himself a community chosen for eternal life and united in true faith. And I believe that I am and always will be a living member of this community. The church is not first a human organisation but something Christ himself is building, and he has promised that the gates of hell will not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18). It reaches across every century and every nation (Revelation 5:9). Notice the personal confidence at the end: not just that the church exists, but that I belong to it, and always will, because Christ holds me. John 10:14–16; Acts 20:28; Romans 10:14–17; Colossians 1:18 Genesis 26:3–4; Revelation 5:9 Isaiah 59:21; 1 Corinthians 11:26 Matthew 16:18; John 10:28–30; Romans 8:28–30; Ephesians 1:3–14 Acts 2:42–47; Ephesians 4:1–6 1 John 3:14, 19–21 John 10:27–28; 1 Corinthians 1:4–9; 1 Peter 1:3–5 What dost thou understand by the communion of saints? First, that believers, all and every one, as members of Christ, have part in him and in all his treasures and gifts. Secondly, that each one must feel himself bound to use his gifts, readily and cheerfully, for the advantage and welfare of other members. First, that believers, one and all, as members of Christ, share in him and in all his treasures and gifts. Second, that each member should know they are duty-bound to use their gifts readily and joyfully for the service and good of the other members. In Christ we receive everything; in the church we give what we have received. No one has all the gifts and no one has none (1 Corinthians 12:4–7). The communion of saints is not a distant ideal but the ordinary, costly love of Christians bearing one another’s burdens (Galatians 6:2) because Christ has borne theirs. Romans 8:32; 1 Corinthians 6:17; 12:4–7, 12–13; 1 John 1:3 Romans 12:4–8; 1 Corinthians 12:20–27; 13:1–7; Philippians 2:4–8 What dost thou believe concerning the forgiveness of sins? That God, for the sake of Christ’s satisfaction, will no more remember my sins, neither the sinful nature with which I have to struggle all my life long; but graciously imparts to me the righteousness of Christ, that I may nevermore come into condemnation. I believe that God, because of Christ’s payment, will never again remember my sins, nor the sinful nature I have to struggle against all my life. Rather, by grace he gives me the righteousness of Christ, so that I will never come into condemnation. This is the sweetest line of the Creed for a troubled conscience. God does not merely overlook our sins; he promises to remember them no more (Jeremiah 31:34), not even the stubborn sinful nature we still fight. And because Christ’s righteousness is given to us, “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Psalm 103:3–4, 10, 12; Micah 7:18–19; 2 Corinthians 5:18–21; 1 John 1:7; 2:2 Romans 7:21–25 John 3:17–18; Romans 8:1–2

Lord’s Day 22: Resurrection and Life Everlasting Part 2: Our Deliverance The Creed ends with the Christian hope. At death the believer’s soul goes at once to Christ; at the last day the body will be raised and made like Christ’s glorious body. Even now we taste the beginning of the joy that will one day be complete. What comfort does the resurrection of the body afford thee? That not only my soul, after this life, shall be immediately taken up to Christ its Head, but also that this my body, raised by the power of Christ, shall again be united with my soul, and made like unto the glorious body of Christ. Not only will my soul be taken immediately after this life to Christ its head, but also this very body of mine, raised by the power of Christ, will be reunited with my soul and made like Christ’s glorious body. Christianity does not despise the body; it promises to redeem it. When a believer dies, they go straight to be with Christ (Luke 23:43), and on the last day their body will be raised, transformed like his (Philippians 3:21). God is not abandoning his creation but making it new, and our bodies are part of that. Luke 16:22; 23:43; Philippians 1:21–23 1 Corinthians 15:20, 42–46, 54; Philippians 3:21; 1 John 3:2 What comfort hast thou from the article of the life everlasting? That, inasmuch as I now feel in my heart the beginning of eternal joy, I shall after this life possess complete bliss, such as eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath entered into the heart of man, therein to praise God forever. That since I now already feel in my heart the beginning of eternal joy, after this life I will have perfect blessedness, such as no eye has seen, no ear has heard and no human heart has ever imagined, in which to praise God for ever. Heaven is not boredom on clouds but the fullness of joy that we only taste now (Psalm 16:11). Every moment of real delight in God is a foretaste of it. And the best part is not the place but the person: we will see God and praise him for ever (1 Corinthians 2:9; Revelation 22:3–4). Romans 14:17 John 17:3; 1 Corinthians 2:9

Lord’s Day 23: Righteous Before God Part 2: Our Deliverance Here the catechism reaches the heart of the Reformation: how can a sinner be right with a holy God? Its answer is breathtaking. Though my conscience accuses me, God, out of sheer grace, counts Christ’s perfect obedience as mine, as if I had never sinned and had obeyed as perfectly as Christ did for me. All I do is accept it with a believing heart. But what does it help thee now that thou believest all this? That I am righteous in Christ before God, and an heir of eternal life. That in Christ I am righteous before God and an heir of eternal life. Believing the Creed is not an intellectual exercise; it changes our standing. The catechism sums up what faith brings in two phrases: right with God now, and heir of everything God has prepared (Romans 5:1; 8:17). Everything else in the Christian life grows out of that secure place. John 3:36; Romans 1:17; 5:1–2 How art thou righteous before God? Only by true faith in Jesus Christ; that is, although my conscience accuse me that I have grievously sinned against all the commandments of God, and have never kept any of them, and that I am still prone always to all evil, yet God, without any merit of mine, of mere grace, grants and imputes to me the perfect satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ, as if I had never committed nor had any sin, and had myself accomplished all the obedience which Christ has fulfilled for me, if only I accept such benefit with a believing heart. Only by true faith in Jesus Christ. Even though my conscience accuses me of having grievously sinned against all God’s commandments, of never having kept any of them, and of still being inclined to all evil, nevertheless, without any merit of my own, out of sheer grace, God gives me and credits to me the perfect payment, righteousness and holiness of Christ, as if I had never sinned nor been a sinner, and as if I had myself carried out all the obedience Christ carried out for me. All I need to do is accept this gift with a believing heart. This may be the most beautiful answer in the catechism. It does not pretend we are better than we are: the accusations of conscience are admitted in full. Yet God gives us Christ’s record as though it were our own, “not having a righteousness of my own... but that which comes through faith in Christ” (Philippians 3:9). We are more sinful than we ever dared admit, and more loved than we ever dared hope. Romans 3:21–28; Galatians 2:16; Ephesians 2:8–9; Philippians 3:8–11 Romans 3:9–10 Romans 7:23 Titus 3:4–5 Romans 3:24; Ephesians 2:8 Romans 4:3–5; 2 Corinthians 5:17–19; 1 John 2:1–2 Romans 4:24–25; 2 Corinthians 5:21 John 3:18; Acts 16:30–31 Why sayest thou that thou art righteous only by faith? Not that I am acceptable to God on account of the worthiness of my faith; but because only the satisfaction, righteousness, and holiness of Christ is my righteousness before God, and I can receive the same and make it my own in no other way than by faith only. Not because my faith makes me acceptable to God, as though it were worth something, but because only Christ’s payment, righteousness and holiness are my righteousness before God, and I can receive that righteousness and make it my own in no other way than by faith alone. Faith is not a new kind of good work that earns God’s approval. It is simply receiving. A drowning man is not saved by the strength of his grip but by the strength of the one who pulled him out. So our assurance does not rest on how strong our faith feels but on how strong our Saviour is (1 John 5:10–12). 1 Corinthians 1:30–31 Romans 10:10; 1 John 5:10–12

Lord’s Day 24: Grace, Good Works and Reward Part 2: Our Deliverance If we are saved by grace alone, what about our good works? The catechism explains that even our best deeds are flawed and could never be our righteousness before God. Yet God graciously rewards them, and true faith always bears fruit. Grace does not make people careless; it makes them grateful. But why can not our good works be the whole or part of our righteousness before God? Because the righteousness which can stand before the judgment-seat of God must be perfect throughout, and wholly conformable to the divine law; whereas even our best works in this life are all imperfect and defiled with sin. Because the righteousness that can stand before God’s judgment must be entirely perfect and must agree in every way with God’s law. But even our best works in this life are all imperfect and stained with sin. Before a holy God, our very best is mixed with pride, self-interest and half-heartedness; “all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment” (Isaiah 64:6). That is not a reason for despair but for relief. We do not have to make our works good enough to save us, because Christ’s work already has. Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:10; Deuteronomy 27:26 Isaiah 64:6 How is it that our good works merit nothing, while yet it is God’s will to reward them in this life and in that which is to come? The reward comes not of merit, but of grace. The reward is not earned; it is a gift of grace. God is so generous that he rewards even the imperfect works he himself worked in us (Philippians 2:13). It is like a father who helps his child make a gift and then thanks the child for it. Every reward in the Christian life is grace upon grace (Luke 17:10). Luke 17:10; 2 Timothy 4:7–8 But does not this doctrine make men careless and profane? No; for it is impossible that those who are implanted into Christ by true faith should not bring forth fruits of righteousness. No. It is impossible for those who have been grafted into Christ by true faith not to produce fruits of thankfulness. Some fear that free grace will make people lazy about holiness. But a branch joined to the vine cannot help bearing fruit (John 15:5). People who know how much they have been forgiven do not look for excuses to sin; they look for ways to show their love (Luke 7:47). Luke 6:43–45; John 15:5

Lord’s Day 25: The Word and the Sacraments Part 2: Our Deliverance Faith is the Spirit’s gift, and he gives it through means. He creates it by the preaching of the gospel, and he strengthens it by the sacraments, which Christ gave as visible signs and seals of his promise. Both point to one place: the sacrifice of Christ on the cross as the only ground of our salvation. Since, then, we are made partakers of Christ and all his benefits by faith only, whence comes this faith? The Holy Ghost works it in our hearts by the preaching of the holy Gospel, and confirms it by the use of the holy Sacraments. The Holy Spirit creates it in our hearts by the preaching of the holy gospel, and strengthens it by the use of the holy sacraments. God does not leave faith to chance. He speaks, and through his word the Spirit opens hearts (Romans 10:17; Acts 16:14). Then, knowing how weak we are, he adds visible signs to his spoken promise, things we can see, touch and taste, so that we might be more sure of his love. John 3:5; 1 Corinthians 2:10–14; Ephesians 2:8 Romans 10:17; 1 Peter 1:23–25 Matthew 28:19–20; 1 Corinthians 10:16 What are the Sacraments? The Sacraments are visible, holy signs and seals, appointed of God for this end, that by the use thereof he may the more fully declare and seal to us the promise of the Gospel; namely, that he grants us out of free grace the forgiveness of sins and everlasting life, for the sake of the one sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross. Sacraments are holy signs and seals that we can see. God instituted them so that by our use of them he might make us understand more clearly the promise of the gospel, and seal that promise to us. And this is the promise: that God freely forgives our sins and gives us eternal life by grace, because of Christ’s one sacrifice finished on the cross. A wedding ring does not create a marriage, but it is a precious and visible pledge of it. In a similar way the sacraments do not save us by themselves; they picture and confirm the promise of the gospel (Romans 4:11). And what they picture is always the same: grace, forgiveness and life, all resting on Christ’s finished work. Genesis 17:11; Deuteronomy 30:6; Romans 4:11 Matthew 26:27–28; Acts 2:38; Hebrews 10:10 Are both these, then, the Word and the sacraments, designed to direct our faith to the sacrifice of Jesus Christ on the cross as the only ground of our salvation? Yes, truly; for the Holy Ghost teaches in the Gospel, and by the holy Sacraments assures us, that our whole salvation stands in the one sacrifice of Christ made for us on the cross. Yes, indeed. In the gospel the Holy Spirit teaches us, and by the holy sacraments he assures us, that our entire salvation rests on Christ’s one sacrifice for us on the cross. Word and sacrament are not rivals but partners, and both have one subject. Every sermon and every celebration of the ordinances is meant to point away from ourselves to the cross (1 Corinthians 2:2). If we leave church looking at our own performance rather than at Christ, something has gone wrong. Romans 6:3; 1 Corinthians 11:26; Galatians 3:27 How many Sacraments has Christ appointed in the New Testament? Two: holy Baptism and the holy Supper. Two: holy baptism and the holy supper. Against the seven sacraments of the medieval church, the Reformers returned to the two that Christ himself commanded: baptism (Matthew 28:19) and the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:23–26). This commentary agrees: Christ gave two ordinances to his church, and each in its own way proclaims his death for us. Matthew 28:19–20; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26

Lord’s Day 26: Holy Baptism Part 2: Our Deliverance Baptism is a picture of the gospel. As water washes the body, so Christ’s blood and Spirit wash the soul, taking away the guilt of sin and making us new. The catechism roots this in Christ’s own command and promise. On this rich meaning of baptism, Baptist and paedobaptist Christians stand on the same ground. How is it signified and sealed unto thee in holy Baptism that thou hast part in the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross? Thus: that Christ has appointed this outward washing with water, and has joined therewith this promise, that I am washed with his blood and Spirit from the pollution of my soul, that is, from all my sins, as certainly as I am washed outwardly with water whereby commonly the filthiness of the body is taken away. In this way: Christ instituted this outward washing with water and joined to it this promise, that I am washed with his blood and Spirit from the uncleanness of my soul, that is, from all my sins, as certainly as I am washed outwardly with water, which normally takes away the dirt of the body. Baptism speaks to the senses about something we cannot see. As surely as the water touched the body, the blood of Christ has cleansed the believer from all sin (1 John 1:7). Martin Luther, in dark moments, is said to have reminded himself that he was baptised; the point was not the ceremony but the promise it pictured. This commentary’s view: we gladly confess all of this, and hold with the 1689 Confession 29 that baptism is a sign of fellowship with Christ in his death and resurrection, given to those who profess repentance and faith, ordinarily by immersion, the picture Paul himself uses of burial and rising (Romans 6:3–4). Matthew 28:19–20; Acts 2:38 Matthew 3:11; Mark 16:16; John 1:33; Romans 6:3–10; 1 Peter 3:21 Mark 1:4; Luke 3:3 What is it to be washed with the blood and Spirit of Christ? It is to have the forgiveness of sins from God, through grace, for the sake of Christ’s blood, which he shed for us in his sacrifice on the cross; and also to be renewed by the Holy Ghost, and sanctified to be members of Christ, that so we may more and more die unto sin, and lead holy and unblamable lives. To be washed with Christ’s blood means that God, by grace, has forgiven my sins because of Christ’s blood, poured out for me in his sacrifice on the cross. To be washed with Christ’s Spirit means that the Holy Spirit has renewed me and set me apart to be a member of Christ, so that more and more I die to sin and live a holy and blameless life. Christ’s washing does two things at once: it takes away our guilt and begins to take away our sin’s power. Forgiveness and renewal always come together, because both come from union with the same Saviour (1 Corinthians 6:11). We are accepted completely, and then changed gradually. Zechariah 13:1; Ephesians 1:7–8; Hebrews 12:24; 1 Peter 1:2; Revelation 1:5; 7:14 Ezekiel 36:25–27; John 3:5–8; Romans 6:4; 1 Corinthians 6:11; Colossians 2:11–12 Where has Christ promised that we are as certainly washed with his blood and Spirit as with the water of Baptism? In the institution of Baptism, which runs thus: Go ye, therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. He that believeth and is baptized, shall be saved; but he that believeth not, shall be damned. This promise is also repeated where the Scripture calls Baptism the washing of regeneration and the washing away of sins. In the institution of baptism, which says: Go therefore and teach all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Whoever believes and is baptised will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned. This promise is repeated where Scripture calls baptism the washing of rebirth and the washing away of sins. Baptism rests on Christ’s own command and promise, not on church tradition (Matthew 28:19). Notice the order in the words the catechism quotes: whoever believes and is baptised (Mark 16:16). Baptism is never a substitute for faith; it is the outward mark of those who have been washed inwardly by the Spirit (Titus 3:5). Matthew 28:19 Mark 16:16 Titus 3:5 Acts 22:16

Lord’s Day 27: Washing and Infant Baptism Part 2: Our Deliverance The water of baptism does not itself wash away sin; only Christ’s blood and Spirit can. Scripture speaks of the sign in the language of the thing it signifies, to assure us that our cleansing is as real as the water. The catechism then argues that the children of believers should be baptised, the point at which this commentary, following the 1689 Confession, respectfully parts company. Is, then, the outward washing of water itself the washing away of sins? No; for only the blood of Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sin. No. Only Jesus Christ’s blood and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sins. This guards against a superstition that has done great harm: the idea that the rite itself saves, whatever the heart. Peter says baptism saves “not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 3:21). The power is in Christ, not in the water, and on this this commentary and the catechism agree completely. Matthew 3:11; 1 Peter 3:21 1 John 1:7; 1 Corinthians 6:11 Why, then, doth the Holy Ghost call Baptism the washing of regeneration and the washing away of sins? God speaks thus not without great cause: namely, not only to teach us thereby that like as the filthiness of the body is taken away by water, so our sins also are taken away by the blood and Spirit of Christ; but much more, that by this divine pledge and token he may assure us that we are as really washed from our sins spiritually as our bodies are washed with water. God has good reason for these words. He wants to teach us that the blood and Spirit of Christ take away our sins just as water takes away the dirt from our bodies. But more important, by this divine pledge and sign he wants to assure us that we are as truly washed of our sins spiritually as our bodies are washed with water. Scripture often speaks of a sign in the language of what it signifies, as when Ananias told Paul to “be baptized and wash away your sins” (Acts 22:16). The sign is so closely tied to the reality that the two can be named together. God uses visible things to reassure doubting hearts that his promise is as real as water on the skin (Revelation 7:14). 1 Corinthians 6:11; Revelation 1:5; 7:14 Acts 2:38; Romans 6:3–4; Galatians 3:27 Are infants also to be baptized? Yes; for since they, as well as their parents, belong to the covenant and people of God, and both redemption from sin and the Holy Ghost, who works faith, are through the blood of Christ promised to them no less than to their parents, they are also by Baptism, as a sign of the covenant, to be ingrafted into the Christian Church, and distinguished from the children of unbelievers, as was done in the Old Testament by Circumcision, in place of which in the New Testament Baptism is appointed. Yes. Infants as well as their parents belong to God’s covenant and people, and they no less than their parents are promised redemption from sin through Christ’s blood and the Holy Spirit who creates faith. Therefore, by baptism, as the sign of the covenant, they too should be received into the Christian church and distinguished from the children of unbelievers. This was done in the Old Testament by circumcision, in whose place baptism has been instituted in the New Testament.
