Behind this answer lies a deep love for children and a confidence that God’s promises run through families: “the promise is for you and for your children” (Acts 2:39), and Abraham’s sons received the covenant sign (Genesis 17:7). Many of the church’s most faithful saints have held this view, and Baptists should understand it fairly and honour those who hold it. This commentary’s view: with the 1689 Confession 29 , this commentary baptises believers only. We share the catechism’s tenderness towards the children of believers, who are set apart by their relation to a believing parent (1 Corinthians 7:14), and its confidence that God saves by his promise and not by the water. But we read the new covenant as one in which every member knows the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11), and Peter’s promise as reaching “everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself” (Acts 2:39). In the New Testament baptism always follows repentance and faith (Acts 2:41; 8:12), and the fulfilment of circumcision is the circumcision of the heart, to which baptism bears witness for those raised with Christ “through faith” (Colossians 2:11–12). So we bring our children to Christ in prayer and teaching, and baptise them gladly when they confess him for themselves. Genesis 17:7; Matthew 19:14 Isaiah 44:1–3; Acts 2:38–39; 16:31 Acts 10:47; 1 Corinthians 7:14 Genesis 17:9–14 Colossians 2:11–13

Lord’s Day 28: The Lord’s Supper Part 2: Our Deliverance In the Supper Christ gives us more than a reminder. As surely as we see the bread broken and taste the cup, his body was broken and his blood shed for us, and he himself nourishes our souls with his crucified body and blood. By the Spirit we are united more and more with the risen Christ in heaven, though we are still on earth. How is it signified and sealed unto thee in the Holy Supper that thou dost partake of the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross and all his benefits? Thus, that Christ has commanded me and all believers to eat of this broken bread, and to drink of this cup, and has joined therewith these promises: First, that his body was offered and broken on the cross for me, and his blood shed for me, as certainly as I see with my eyes the bread of the Lord broken for me, and the cup communicated to me; and, further, that with his crucified body and shed blood he himself feeds and nourishes my soul to everlasting life, as certainly as I receive from the hand of the minister, and taste with my mouth, the bread and cup of the Lord, which are given me as certain tokens of the body and blood of Christ. In this way: Christ has commanded me and all believers to eat this broken bread and drink this cup in remembrance of him. With this command he has given these promises. First, as surely as I see with my eyes the bread of the Lord broken for me and the cup shared with me, so surely was his body offered and broken for me and his blood poured out for me on the cross. Second, as surely as I receive from the hand of the minister and taste with my mouth the bread and cup of the Lord, given me as sure signs of Christ’s body and blood, so surely does he himself nourish and refresh my soul for eternal life with his crucified body and poured-out blood. The Supper is an act of God’s kindness to people who forget easily and doubt often. Every time the bread is broken, the gospel is preached to our eyes: “as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). And it is not only a looking back; Christ himself feeds our souls, as truly as bread feeds the body (John 6:35). Matthew 26:26–28; Mark 14:22–24; Luke 22:19–20; 1 Corinthians 11:23–25 What is it to eat the crucified body and drink the shed blood of Christ? It is not only to embrace with a believing heart all the sufferings and death of Christ, and thereby to obtain the forgiveness of sins and life eternal, but moreover, also, to be so united more and more to his sacred body by the Holy Ghost, who dwells both in Christ and in us, that although he is in heaven, and we on the earth, we are nevertheless flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones, and live and are governed forever by one Spirit, as members of the same body are by one soul. It means not only to accept with a believing heart all the suffering and death of Christ, and so to receive forgiveness of sins and eternal life. It means also to be united more and more to his blessed body by the Holy Spirit, who lives both in Christ and in us. So although Christ is in heaven and we are on earth, we are nevertheless flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones, and we live and are ruled for ever by one Spirit, as the members of one body are ruled by one soul. Communion with Christ is real, not imaginary. The Spirit who lives in Christ and in us bridges the distance between heaven and earth, so that we are truly joined to the risen Lord (1 Corinthians 6:17). This commentary holds this Reformed view gladly: Christ is truly present by his Spirit, and believers feed on him by faith, while the bread and wine remain what they are. John 6:35, 40, 50–54 John 6:55–56; 1 Corinthians 12:13 Acts 1:9–11; 1 Corinthians 11:26; Colossians 3:1 1 Corinthians 6:15–17; Ephesians 5:29–30; 1 John 4:13 John 6:56–58; 15:1–6; Ephesians 4:15–16; 1 John 3:24 Where has Christ promised that he will thus feed and nourish believers with his body and blood, as certainly as they eat of this broken bread and drink of this cup? In the institution of the Supper, which runs thus: The Lord Jesus, the same night in which he was betrayed, took bread; and when he had given thanks, he brake it and said: ‘Take, eat, this is my body, which is broken for you; this do in remembrance of me.’ After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood; this do ye as often as ye drink it, in remembrance of me. For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do show the Lord’s death till he come.’ And this promise is repeated also by St. Paul, where he says: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? For we, being many, are one bread, and one body; for we are all partakers of that one bread. In the institution of the Supper, which says: The Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, Take, eat; this is my body, which is broken for you; do this in remembrance of me. In the same way he also took the cup, after supper, saying, This cup is the new covenant in my blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me. For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. This promise is repeated by Paul, where he says: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all share the one bread. The Supper was given on the night of betrayal, which tells us it is for people who fail. Jesus knew what his friends were about to do, and he fed them anyway. And the Supper binds us not only to Christ but to one another, since “we who are many are one body” (1 Corinthians 10:17). 1 Corinthians 11:23–26 1 Corinthians 10:16–17

Lord’s Day 29: Signs, Not Substance Part 2: Our Deliverance Against the medieval teaching that the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood, the catechism holds that they remain bread and wine. Yet they are not empty symbols. Christ calls them his body and blood to assure us that, by the Holy Spirit, we really share in him and all he has done, as surely as we eat and drink. Do, then, the bread and wine become the real body and blood of Christ? No; but as the water in Baptism is not changed into the blood of Christ, nor becomes the washing away of sins itself, being only the divine token and assurance thereof, so also in the Lord’s Supper the sacred bread does not become the body of Christ itself, though agreeably to the nature and usage of sacraments it is called the body of Christ. No. Just as the water of baptism is not changed into Christ’s blood and does not itself wash away sins, but is only God’s sign and assurance of it, so also the holy bread of the Lord’s Supper does not become Christ’s body itself, even though, in keeping with the nature and language of sacraments, it is called the body of Christ. Jesus often spoke in pictures, calling himself the door and the vine (John 10:9; 15:1). When he said “This is my body”, he was giving a sign so closely tied to its reality that it bears its name. The bread remains bread, and Christ’s body remains in heaven (Acts 3:21). This commentary agrees: the Supper is a real communion with Christ, not a change in the elements. Ephesians 5:26; Titus 3:5 Matthew 26:26–29 1 Corinthians 10:1–4; 1 Peter 3:21 1 Corinthians 11:26–28 Why, then, doth Christ call the bread his body, and the cup his blood, or the New Testament in his blood; and St. Paul, the communion of the body and blood of Christ? Christ speaks thus not without great cause: namely, not only to teach us thereby that like as bread and wine sustain this temporal life, so also his crucified body and shed blood are the true meat and drink of our souls unto life eternal; but much more, by this visible sign and pledge to assure us that we are as really partakers of his true body and blood, through the working of the Holy Ghost, as we receive by the mouth of the body these holy tokens in remembrance of him; and that all his sufferings and obedience are as certainly our own as if we had ourselves suffered and done all in our own persons. Christ has good reason for these words. He wants to teach us that, as bread and wine nourish our earthly life, so his crucified body and poured-out blood are the true food and drink of our souls for eternal life. But more important, by these visible signs and pledges he wants to assure us that, through the Holy Spirit’s work, we share in his true body and blood as surely as we receive these holy signs with our mouths in remembrance of him; and that all his suffering and obedience are as certainly ours as if we had suffered and done everything ourselves. The last line of this answer is one of the great comforts of the catechism: Christ’s obedience and suffering are counted ours as if we had done them ourselves. At the table we receive not just bread and wine but the assurance that Christ is ours and we are his. “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35), he says, and in the Supper he gives himself. John 6:51, 55 1 Corinthians 10:16–17; 11:26 Romans 6:5–11

Lord’s Day 30: The Supper and the Mass; Who May Come Part 2: Our Deliverance This Lord’s Day contrasts the Lord’s Supper with the Mass of its day, and then asks who should come to the table. The answer is full of grace: not those who think themselves good enough, but those who grieve over their sins and trust that Christ has covered them. Those who show by word and life that they are unbelieving and impenitent are to be kept from it, for their own good and the honour of Christ. What difference is there between the Lord’s Supper and the Popish Mass? The Lord’s Supper testifies to us that we have full forgiveness of all our sins by the one sacrifice of Jesus Christ, which he himself has once accomplished on the cross; [and that by the Holy Ghost we are ingrafted into Christ, who with his true body is now in heaven at the right hand of the Father, and is to be there worshiped]. But the Mass teaches that the living and the dead have not forgiveness of sins through the sufferings of Christ unless Christ is still daily offered for them by the priests; [and that Christ is bodily under the form of bread and wine, and is therefore to be worshiped in them]. And thus the Mass at bottom is nothing else than a denial of the one sacrifice and passion of Jesus Christ [and an accursed idolatry]. The Lord’s Supper declares to us that all our sins are completely forgiven through the one sacrifice of Jesus Christ, which he himself finished on the cross once for all; and that through the Holy Spirit we are grafted into Christ, who with his true body is now in heaven at the right hand of the Father, where he wants us to worship him. But the Mass teaches that the living and the dead do not have their sins forgiven through the suffering of Christ unless Christ is still offered for them daily by the priests; and that Christ is bodily present in the form of bread and wine, and is therefore to be worshipped in them. And so the Mass is basically nothing but a denial of the one sacrifice and suffering of Jesus Christ, and an accursed idolatry. The heart of this answer is a joyful truth: Christ’s sacrifice is finished. “When Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12), and nothing can be added to it. A priest who stands daily at an altar would imply that the work is not done; a Saviour who sits shows that it is. This commentary’s view: this question was not in the first edition of 1563. It was added in the second edition, and its sharpest words, including the closing phrase, in the third, as the Council of Trent was defining the Mass as a true sacrifice (the bracketed words in the historic text mark these later additions). This commentary shares its conviction that Christ’s sacrifice is once for all, never repeated or added to, and that the Supper is no sacrifice and the Lord’s Table no altar. Its language belongs to a fierce age, and some Reformed churches now print a note beside it. We should speak with the same clarity about the doctrine while remembering that it judges a teaching, not the heart of every person who attends Mass, and that many Roman Catholics love the Lord Jesus. John 19:30; Hebrews 7:27; 9:12, 25–26; 10:10–18 1 Corinthians 6:17; 10:16–17 John 20:17; Acts 7:55–56; Hebrews 1:3; 8:1 Matthew 6:20–21; John 4:21–24; Philippians 3:20; Colossians 3:1–3 Hebrews 9:26; 10:12–14 Who are to come unto the table of the Lord? Those who are displeased with themselves for their sins, yet trust that these are forgiven them, and that their remaining infirmity is covered by the passion and death of Christ; who also desire more and more to strengthen their faith and amend their life. But the impenitent and hypocrites eat and drink judgment to themselves. Those who are displeased with themselves because of their sins, but who nevertheless trust that their sins are forgiven them and that their remaining weakness is covered by the suffering and death of Christ, and who also desire more and more to strengthen their faith and to improve their life. But the unrepentant and hypocrites eat and drink judgment on themselves. The table is not for the spiritually impressive but for sinners who know their need and trust their Saviour. If you come grieving over your sin and longing to grow, you are exactly the kind of person Christ invites (Matthew 11:28). What Paul warns against is coming carelessly, while clinging to sin and despising what the Supper means (1 Corinthians 11:27–29). 1 Corinthians 10:19–22; 11:26–32 Are they, then, also to be admitted to this Supper who show themselves to be, by their confession and life, unbelieving and ungodly? No; for by this the covenant of God is profaned, and his wrath provoked against the whole congregation; wherefore the Christian Church is bound, according to the order of Christ and his Apostles, by the office of the keys to exclude such person until they amend their life. No. That would dishonour God’s covenant and bring down God’s anger on the whole congregation. Therefore, according to the command of Christ and his apostles, the Christian church is duty-bound to exclude such people, by the official use of the keys of the kingdom, until they reform their lives. Guarding the table is not about keeping people out but about telling them the truth, in love, so that they might come back (1 Corinthians 5:5). A church that welcomes anyone to the Supper regardless of their life is not more loving but less, because it lets people believe they are safe when they are not. This commentary agrees that the table is for baptised believers who trust Christ and are not under discipline. 1 Corinthians 11:17–32; Psalm 50:14–16; Isaiah 1:11–17

Lord’s Day 31: The Keys of the Kingdom Part 2: Our Deliverance Christ gave his church two keys: the preaching of the gospel and church discipline. By them the kingdom is opened to those who believe and shut to those who refuse. Both are acts of love, and both aim at the same thing, that sinners might find and keep the forgiveness of sins in Christ. What is the Office of the Keys? The preaching of the holy Gospel and Church discipline; by which two things the kingdom of heaven is opened to believers and shut against unbelievers. The preaching of the holy gospel and church discipline. By these two the kingdom of heaven is opened to believers and closed to unbelievers. Jesus gave Peter “the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:19), and the Reformers saw those keys in the ordinary ministry of every faithful church. The keys are not magic powers but the authority of Christ’s word. When the gospel is faithfully preached, the door of heaven really opens. Matthew 16:19; John 20:22–23 How is the kingdom of heaven opened and shut by the preaching of the holy Gospel? In this way: that, according to the command of Christ, it is proclaimed and openly witnessed to believers, one and all, that as often as they accept with true faith the promise of the Gospel, all their sins are really forgiven them of God for the sake of Christ’s merits; and on the contrary, to all unbelievers and hypocrites, that the wrath of God and eternal condemnation abide on them so long as they are not converted: according to which witness of the Gospel will be the judgment of God, both in this life and in that which is to come. According to the command of Christ, the kingdom of heaven is opened by proclaiming and publicly declaring to all believers, each and every one, that whenever they accept the gospel promise in true faith, God really forgives all their sins because of what Christ has done. The kingdom of heaven is closed, however, by proclaiming and declaring to all unbelievers and hypocrites that, as long as they do not repent, the anger of God and eternal condemnation rest on them. God’s judgment, both in this life and in the life to come, is based on this gospel testimony. Every faithful sermon is an act of heaven. When a preacher says, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31), that is not a human opinion but God’s own word of welcome. And the warning is also love, because it calls people back while there is still time (John 20:23). John 20:21–23 John 3:31–36; Acts 16:31 Matthew 16:19; Romans 2:2–17 How is the kingdom of heaven shut and opened by Church discipline? In this way: that, according to the command of Christ, if any under the Christian name show themselves unsound either in doctrine or life, and after repeated brotherly admonition refuse to turn from their errors or evil ways, they are complained of to the Church or to its proper officers, and, if they neglect to hear them also, are by them excluded from the holy Sacraments and the Christian communion, and by God himself from the kingdom of Christ; and if they promise and show real amendment, they are again received as members of Christ and his Church. According to the command of Christ, those who call themselves Christians but show that they are unsound in doctrine or life are first warned repeatedly in a brotherly way. If they do not give up their errors or wickedness, they are reported to the church, that is, to those appointed by the church. Then, if they do not listen to them either, they are excluded by them from the holy sacraments and the Christian fellowship, and by God himself from the kingdom of Christ. But if they promise and show real amendment, they are received again as members of Christ and his church. Church discipline sounds harsh, but its goal is always restoration (Galatians 6:1). Jesus described a careful, patient process that begins privately and goes public only if needed (Matthew 18:15–20). And the door is always open: anyone who repents is to be welcomed back with joy (2 Corinthians 2:6–8). Matthew 18:15–20 1 Corinthians 5:3–5, 11–13; 2 Thessalonians 3:14–15 Luke 15:20–24; 2 Corinthians 2:6–11

Lord’s Day 32: Why Good Works? Part 3: Our Thankfulness The third part of the catechism is about gratitude, and it begins with the obvious question: if we are saved by grace without any merit of our own, why do good works? Not to earn anything, the catechism replies, but because Christ, who bought us, is also making us new, so that our whole life becomes a thank-you to God, an assurance to ourselves and a witness to our neighbours. Since, then, we are redeemed from our misery by grace through Christ, without any merit of ours, why must we do good works? Because Christ, having redeemed us by his blood, renews us also by his holy Spirit after his own image, that with our whole life we may show ourselves thankful to God for his blessing, and that he may be glorified through us; then, also, that we ourselves may be assured of our faith by the fruits thereof, and by our godly walk may win our neighbors also to Christ. Because Christ, having set us free by his blood, is also renewing us by his Holy Spirit into his image, so that with our whole lives we may show that we are thankful to God for his goodness, and that he may be praised through us. Further, so that we may be assured of our faith by its fruits, and so that by our godly living we may win our neighbours for Christ. Here is the root of Christian obedience: not fear, not pride, but gratitude. We do good not to be loved but because we are loved (1 John 4:19). And a life changed by grace becomes a quiet argument for the gospel, as Jesus said, so that others “may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). Romans 6:13; 12:1–2; 1 Peter 2:5–10 Matthew 5:16; 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 Matthew 7:17–18; Galatians 5:22–24; 2 Peter 1:10–11 Matthew 5:14–16; Romans 14:17–19; 1 Peter 2:12; 3:1–2 Can they, then, not be saved who do not turn to God from their unthankful, impenitent life? By no means; for, as the Scripture saith, no unchaste person, idolater, adulterer, thief, covetous man, drunkard, slanderer, robber, or any such like, shall inherit the kingdom of God. By no means. Scripture says that no unchaste person, idolater, adulterer, thief, greedy person, drunkard, slanderer, robber or the like will inherit the kingdom of God. Grace is free, but it is not powerless. Those who go on living for themselves without repentance show they have never truly known the grace they claim (1 John 3:6). Yet the same passage the catechism echoes goes on to say “And such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11): no one is beyond the reach of the grace that changes lives. 1 Corinthians 6:9–10; Galatians 5:19–21; Ephesians 5:1–20; 1 John 3:14

Lord’s Day 33: True Conversion Part 3: Our Thankfulness True repentance has two sides: the dying of the old self, which is genuine sorrow for sin and a turning from it, and the coming to life of the new, which is wholehearted joy in God and delight in doing his will. Good works, then, are not whatever we think good, but what flows from faith, follows God’s law and aims at his glory. In how many things does true repentance or conversion consist? In two things: the dying of the old man, and the quickening of the new. Two things: the dying away of the old self and the coming to life of the new. The Christian life is not self-improvement but death and resurrection, the pattern of Christ himself worked out in us (Romans 6:4–6). Something has to die: our self-rule, our old loves. And something wonderful comes to life in its place. Both happen not once but every day. Romans 6:1–11; 2 Corinthians 5:17; Ephesians 4:22–24; Colossians 3:5–10 What is the dying of the old man? Heartfelt sorrow for sin; causing us to hate and turn from it always more and more. Heartfelt sorrow for sin, which makes us hate it more and more and run away from it. Real repentance is not just regret at being caught or fear of punishment. It is grief at having wronged the God who loves us, a “godly grief” that “produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret” (2 Corinthians 7:10). And that grief gradually changes what we love, so that sin loses its appeal. Psalm 51:3–4, 17; Joel 2:12–13; Romans 8:12–13; 2 Corinthians 7:10 What is the quickening of the new man? Heartfelt joy in God; causing us to take delight in living according to the will of God in all good works. Wholehearted joy in God through Christ, which makes us love to live according to the will of God in all good works. The Christian life is not only saying no; it is mostly a deeper yes. Joy in God is the engine of holiness, because we will always end up doing what we most delight in (Psalm 37:4). When God himself becomes our joy, obedience becomes less a burden and more a delight. Psalm 51:8, 12; Isaiah 57:15; Romans 5:1; 14:17 Romans 6:10–11; Galatians 2:20 But what are good works? Those only which are done from true faith, according to the law of God, for his glory; and not such as rest on our own opinion or the commandments of men. Only those which are done out of true faith, in keeping with God’s law, and for his glory; and not those based on our own opinion or on human commands. Good works are not defined by what impresses people or what we think religious. They spring from trust in God (Hebrews 11:6), follow what he has actually said, and aim at his honour rather than ours (1 Corinthians 10:31). This frees us from man-made rules that Christ never laid on anyone (Matthew 15:9). John 15:5; Hebrews 11:6 Leviticus 18:4; 1 Samuel 15:22; Ephesians 2:10 1 Corinthians 10:31 Deuteronomy 12:32; Isaiah 29:13; Ezekiel 20:18–19; Matthew 15:7–9

Lord’s Day 34: The Law of God; the First Commandment Part 3: Our Thankfulness The catechism teaches the Ten Commandments in the part about thankfulness, not misery. That placement says something wonderful: the law is the shape of a grateful life. It begins with the words of redemption, I am the Lord your God who brought you out of slavery, and the first commandment calls us to trust, love and honour the one true God above all. What is the law of God? God spake all these words, saying: I am the Lord thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt have no other gods before me. Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth; thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them. For I the Lord thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me; and showing mercy unto thousands of them that love me and keep my commandments. Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain; for the Lord will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain. Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labor, and do all thy work: but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord thy God; in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy man-servant, nor thy maid-servant, nor thy cattle, nor the stranger that is within thy gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day; wherefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day, and hallowed it. Honor thy father and thy mother; that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee. Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor. Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor’s house; thou shalt not covet thy neighbor’s wife, nor his man-servant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbor’s. God spoke all these words: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything in heaven above, on the earth beneath or in the water under the earth; you shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the Lord your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments. You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain. Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labour and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God; on it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the stranger who is within your gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day; therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy. Honour your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the Lord your God is giving you. You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour. You shall not covet your neighbour’s house; you shall not covet your neighbour’s wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbour’s. Notice how the law begins: not with a command but with a rescue. God first says who he is and what he has done, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 20:2), and only then how his freed people should live. That is the gospel order: grace first, then obedience as the grateful response of the redeemed. Exodus 20:1–17; Deuteronomy 5:6–21 How are these Commandments divided? Into two tables: the first of which teaches us, in four commandments, what duties we owe to God; the second, in six, what duties we owe to our neighbor. Into two tables. The first teaches us, in four commandments, how we are to live in relation to God; the second, in six commandments, what we owe our neighbour. Jesus summed up the law in the same two parts: love God, and love your neighbour (Matthew 22:37–39). The two cannot be separated. Love for God shows itself in love for people, and love for people is deepest when it flows from love for God (1 John 4:20–21). Matthew 22:37–39 Matthew 22:39; Romans 13:8–10 What does God require in the first commandment? That, on peril of my soul’s salvation, I avoid and flee all idolatry, sorcery, enchantments, invocation of saints or of other creatures; and that I rightly acknowledge the only true God, trust in him alone, with all humility and patience expect all good from him only, and love, fear, and honor him with my whole heart; so as rather to renounce all creatures than do the least thing against his will. That for the sake of my very salvation I avoid and run from all idolatry, sorcery, superstitious rites, and prayer to saints or to other creatures. That I rightly know the only true God, trust him alone, look to him for every good thing humbly and patiently, and love, fear and honour him with all my heart. In short, that I give up anything rather than go against his will in the slightest way. Everyone worships something; the question is what. The first commandment calls us to give our ultimate trust and love only to the one who deserves it. This is not a narrowing of life but a liberation, because every other god eventually enslaves and disappoints us, and only the true God loves us back (1 John 5:21). 1 Corinthians 6:9–10; 10:5–14; 1 John 5:21 Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:9–12 Matthew 4:10; Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9 John 17:3 Jeremiah 17:5, 7 1 Peter 5:5–6 Colossians 1:11; Hebrews 10:36 James 1:17 Deuteronomy 6:5; Matthew 22:37 Deuteronomy 6:2; Psalm 111:10; Proverbs 1:7; 9:10; Matthew 10:28 Matthew 4:10 Matthew 5:29–30; 10:37–39 What is idolatry? It is, instead of the one true God who has revealed himself in his Word, or along with the same, to conceive or have something else on which to place our trust. Idolatry is having or inventing something in which to put our trust instead of, or in addition to, the one true God who has revealed himself in his Word. This definition is searching, because it shows that idolatry is not just bowing to statues. Anything we rely on for our deepest security, money, success, a relationship, our own goodness, can become a god (Colossians 3:5). The cure is not merely tearing idols down but finding in Christ something more beautiful than all of them. 1 Chronicles 16:26; Galatians 4:8–9; Ephesians 5:5; Philippians 3:19

Lord’s Day 35: The Second Commandment Part 3: Our Thankfulness The first commandment tells us whom to worship; the second tells us how. God is not to be pictured or worshipped in ways we invent, but only as he has commanded in his Word. The catechism holds that God has chosen to teach his people not by images but by the living preaching of his Word. What does God require in the second commandment? That we in nowise make any image of God, nor worship him in any other way than he has commanded in his Word. That we in no way make any image of God, nor worship him in any other way than he has commanded in his Word. We cannot capture God in an image without shrinking him to our own size. He has shown us what he is like in his Word and, supremely, in his Son, “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). Worship that follows his Word is not cramped but safe, because it keeps us meeting the real God and not one we have made up. Deuteronomy 4:15–19; Isaiah 40:18–25; Acts 17:29; Romans 1:22–23 Leviticus 10:1–7; 1 Samuel 15:22–23; John 4:23–24 Must we, then, not make any image at all? God may not and can not be imaged in any way; as for creatures, though they may indeed be imaged, yet God forbids the making or keeping any likeness of them, either to worship them, or by them to serve himself. God cannot and may not be portrayed in any way. As for creatures, although they may indeed be portrayed, God forbids making or having any images of them in order to worship them or to use them to serve him. The catechism is not against art. Creatures may be depicted, and the beauty of painting and sculpture is a gift. What God forbids is using images in worship, as though they could bring us nearer to him (Exodus 20:4–5). He has given us his Word and his Spirit, and in them he comes near himself. Isaiah 40:25 Exodus 34:13–14, 17; 2 Kings 18:4–5 But may not pictures be tolerated in churches as books for the laity? No; for we should not be wiser than God, who will not have his people taught by dumb idols, but by the lively preaching of his Word. No. We should not try to be wiser than God. He wants his people to be taught not by lifeless idols but by the living preaching of his Word. The medieval church had defended images as books for people who could not read. The Reformers answered that God had appointed a better teacher: his Word, preached by living voices (Romans 10:14–17). Faith comes by hearing. This commentary’s view: this commentary follows the same Reformed caution, and holds that no image of Christ should be used in worship or as an aid to prayer. Many Christians believe that, because Christ took a real body, he may be depicted, and they should be heard with respect; but we would rather meet him where he has promised to be found, in his Word and in the gathered church. Jeremiah 10:8; Habakkuk 2:18–20 Romans 10:14–17; 2 Timothy 3:16–17; 2 Peter 1:19

Lord’s Day 36: The Third Commandment Part 3: Our Thankfulness God’s name is his self-revelation, all that he has shown us of who he is. To use it carelessly, in cursing, false oaths or idle swearing, is to treat God himself as cheap. The catechism adds that silence when others misuse it makes us share in the sin. Positively, the name of God is to be used only with reverence, so that he is rightly confessed and praised in all we say and do. What is required in the third commandment? That we must not by cursing, or by false swearing, nor yet by unnecessary oaths, profane or abuse the name of God; nor even by our silence and connivance be partakers of these horrible sins in others; and in sum, that we use the holy name of God no otherwise than with fear and reverence, so that he may be rightly confessed and worshiped by us, and be glorified in all our words and works. That we must not profane or abuse the name of God by cursing, by perjury or by unnecessary oaths, nor share in such horrible sins by being silent bystanders. In short, that we use the holy name of God only with fear and reverence, so that we may rightly confess him, call on him and praise him in everything we say and do. How we speak of God reveals what we really think of him. The commandment forbids not only obvious blasphemy but the casual, empty use of his name, as if he were a word to fill a silence. Positively, it calls us to speak of him the way people speak of someone they love and revere (Psalm 8:1; Colossians 3:17). Leviticus 24:10–17 Leviticus 19:12 Matthew 5:37; James 5:12 Leviticus 5:1; Proverbs 29:24 Psalm 99:1–5; Jeremiah 4:2 Matthew 10:32–33; Romans 10:9–10 Psalm 50:14–15; 1 Timothy 2:8 Colossians 3:17 Is, then, the profaning of God’s name, by swearing and cursing, so grievous a sin that his wrath is kindled against those also who seek not, as much as in them lies, to hinder and forbid the same? Yes, truly; for no sin is greater or more provoking to God than the profaning of his name. Wherefore he even commanded it to be punished with death. Yes, indeed. No sin is greater or provokes God more than the misuse of his name. That is why he commanded it to be punished with death. The death penalty for blasphemy belonged to the law of Israel as a nation under God (Leviticus 24:16), and the catechism cites it to show how seriously God takes his name, not to ask the state to enforce it today. The deeper point is that God’s name is precious to him because it is his very self. Jesus taught us to begin our prayers by asking that it be “hallowed” (Matthew 6:9). Leviticus 5:1 Leviticus 24:10–17

Lord’s Day 37: Lawful Oaths Part 3: Our Thankfulness May a Christian ever swear an oath? The catechism says yes, when the government requires it or when it is needed to uphold faithfulness and truth, to God’s glory and our neighbour’s good. But we must never swear by saints or any creature, because an oath calls on God alone, who sees the heart, as witness. But may we not swear by the name of God in a religious manner? Yes; when the magistrate requires it, or it may be needful otherwise to maintain and promote fidelity and truth, to the glory of God and our neighbor’s good. For such swearing is grounded in God’s Word, and therefore was rightly used by the saints in the Old and New Testament. Yes, when the government requires it, or when it is otherwise necessary to maintain and promote faithfulness and truth, for God’s glory and our neighbour’s good. Such oaths are grounded in God’s Word and were rightly used by the saints in the Old and New Testaments. Jesus forbade the casual swearing that made truthfulness depend on oaths (Matthew 5:33–37), but Scripture shows God himself swearing (Hebrews 6:16–17) and Paul calling God to witness (2 Corinthians 1:23). A solemn oath in a court, or a marriage vow, can honour God. The aim is a life so truthful that our ordinary yes means yes. Deuteronomy 6:13; 10:20; Jeremiah 4:1–2; Hebrews 6:16 Genesis 21:24; Joshua 9:15; 1 Kings 1:29–30; Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23 May we swear by the saints or any other creatures? No; for a lawful oath is a calling upon God, as the only searcher of hearts, to bear witness to the truth, and to punish me if I swear falsely; which honor is due to no creature. No. A lawful oath calls on God, as the only one who knows the heart, to witness to the truth and to punish me if I swear falsely. No creature is worthy of such honour. An oath appeals to the one who sees what no one else can (Psalm 139:1–4). To swear by a saint or by any created thing gives it an honour that belongs to God alone. Only God searches hearts, and only he can be trusted as the final judge of truth (Jeremiah 17:10). Romans 9:1; 2 Corinthians 1:23 Matthew 5:34–37; 23:16–22; James 5:12

Lord’s Day 38: The Fourth Commandment Part 3: Our Thankfulness The catechism’s answer on the fourth commandment is notably gentle. It speaks of supporting the ministry of the gospel, gladly gathering for worship on the day of rest, and above all resting from our sinful works every day so that God may work in us, beginning here the eternal Sabbath. It is a vision of rest as a gift, not a burden. What does God require in the fourth commandment? In the first place, that the ministry of the Gospel and schools be maintained; and that I, especially on the day of rest, diligently attend church, to learn the Word of God, to use the holy Sacraments, to call publicly upon the Lord, and to give Christian alms. In the second place, that all the days of my life I rest from my evil works, allow the Lord to work in me by his Spirit, and thus begin in this life the everlasting Sabbath. First, that the ministry of the gospel and the schools be maintained, and that I, especially on the day of rest, diligently attend the gathering of God’s people, to learn God’s Word, to use the holy sacraments, to call publicly on the Lord and to give Christian offerings for the poor. Second, that every day of my life I rest from my evil works, let the Lord work in me through his Spirit, and so begin in this life the eternal Sabbath. The Sabbath was always about rest in God, and in Christ that rest has come: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Gathering with God’s people is not a duty to be endured but a feast to be enjoyed, and the deepest rest is ceasing from our own efforts to save ourselves (Hebrews 4:9–10). This commentary’s view: this commentary finds the catechism’s answer close to its own. It holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ and that the Lord’s Day is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest out of joy and wisdom, not a law with rules about work, and that no one may bind another’s conscience about days (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly Christians, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, and they are honoured brothers and sisters. Deuteronomy 6:4–9, 20–25; 1 Corinthians 9:13–14; 2 Timothy 2:2; 3:13–17; Titus 1:5 Deuteronomy 12:5–12; Psalm 40:9–10; 68:26; Acts 2:42–47; Hebrews 10:23–25 Romans 10:14–17; 1 Corinthians 14:31–32; 1 Timothy 4:13 1 Corinthians 11:23–24 Colossians 3:16; 1 Timothy 2:1 Psalm 50:14; 1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8–9 Isaiah 66:23; Hebrews 4:9–11

Lord’s Day 39: The Fifth Commandment Part 3: Our Thankfulness God governs us through human authority, beginning with our parents. The fifth commandment calls for honour, love and faithfulness towards father and mother and all in authority over us, willing submission to their good teaching and correction, and patience with their weaknesses, because it is God’s will to lead us by their hand. What does God require in the fifth commandment? That I show all honor, love, and faithfulness to my father and mother, and to all in authority over me; submit myself with due obedience to all their good instruction and correction, and also bear patiently with their infirmities, since it is God’s will to govern us by their hand. That I show honour, love and faithfulness to my father and mother and to all who are set in authority over me; that I submit with proper obedience to all their good teaching and correction; and also that I be patient with their failings, since it is God’s will to govern us by their hand. No parent or leader is perfect, and the catechism wisely asks us to bear patiently with their weaknesses. Honour is not blind obedience; we must obey God rather than men when the two conflict (Acts 5:29). But it is a recognition that God gives authority as a gift for our good, and that honouring our parents is part of honouring him. It is “the first commandment with a promise” (Ephesians 6:2). Lord’s Day 40: The Sixth Commandment Part 3: Our Thankfulness The sixth commandment reaches far deeper than physical murder. It forbids every attack on our neighbour, in thought, word, look or deed, and the roots of murder in envy, hatred, anger and the desire for revenge. Positively, it calls us to patience, peace, gentleness, mercy and kindness, even towards our enemies. What does God require in the sixth commandment? That I neither in thought, nor in word or look, much less in deed, revile, hate, insult, or kill my neighbor, whether by myself or by another; but lay aside all desire of revenge: moreover, that I harm not myself, nor willfully run into any danger. Wherefore, also, to restrain murder, the magistrate is armed with the sword. That I do not dishonour, hate, injure or kill my neighbour, whether in thought, word or gesture, much less in deed, either by myself or through another; but that I lay aside all desire for revenge. Also, that I do not harm myself or recklessly put myself in danger. That is why, to restrain murder, the government is armed with the sword. Every human life bears God’s image, and so every life is precious (Genesis 9:6). That includes our own, which is why the commandment also forbids self-harm and needless risk. And because God takes life so seriously, he has given governments the sword to protect the innocent (Romans 13:4), while forbidding us to take personal revenge. Genesis 9:6; Leviticus 19:17–18; Matthew 5:21–22; 26:52 Proverbs 25:21–22; Matthew 18:35; Romans 12:19; Ephesians 4:26 Matthew 4:7; 26:52; Romans 13:11–14 Genesis 9:6; Exodus 21:14; Romans 13:4 But this commandment speaks only of killing. In forbidding this, however, God means to teach us that he abhors the root of murder—namely, envy, hatred, anger, and desire of revenge; and that all these are in his sight hidden murder. By forbidding murder God teaches us that he hates the root of murder: envy, hatred, anger and the desire for revenge. In his sight all these are hidden murder. Jesus said the same: anger and contempt are murder in the heart (Matthew 5:21–22). That should humble every one of us. But it also points us to the cross, where the one we wronged absorbed our hatred and answered it with forgiveness (Luke 23:34). Proverbs 14:30; Romans 1:29; 12:19; Galatians 5:19–21; 1 John 2:9–11 1 John 3:15 Is it, then, enough that we do not kill our neighbor in any such way? No; for in condemning envy, hatred, and anger, God requires us to love our neighbor as ourselves, to show patience, peace, meekness, mercy, and kindness towards him, and, so far as we have power, to prevent his hurt; also, to do good even unto our enemies. No. By condemning envy, hatred and anger, God commands us to love our neighbour as ourselves, to be patient, peaceable, gentle, merciful and friendly towards him, to protect him from harm as far as we can, and to do good even to our enemies. It is not enough to avoid harming people; God calls us to seek their good. This is impossible for us on our own, especially the command to love enemies (Matthew 5:44). But we were God’s enemies when Christ died for us (Romans 5:10), and that undeserved love is what makes love for enemies possible. Matthew 7:12; 22:39; Romans 12:10 Matthew 5:3–12; Luke 6:36; Romans 12:10, 18; Galatians 6:1–2; Ephesians 4:2; Colossians 3:12; 1 Peter 3:8 Exodus 23:4–5; Matthew 5:44–45; Romans 12:20–21

Lord’s Day 41: The Seventh Commandment Part 3: Our Thankfulness God made our bodies and our sexuality good, and the seventh commandment protects that gift. All unchastity is condemned, and we are called to live purely, whether married or single. Because body and soul are temples of the Holy Spirit, God’s concern reaches past outward acts to our gestures, words, thoughts and desires. What does the seventh commandment teach us? That all unchastity is accursed of God; and that we should therefore loathe it from the heart, and live chastely and modestly, whether in holy wedlock or single life. That all unchastity is cursed by God, and that we should therefore hate it with all our heart and live chaste and disciplined lives, whether in holy marriage or in single life. God’s limits on sex are not the rules of a killjoy but the protection of something precious. Sex is meant to express and seal the lifelong, faithful self-giving of marriage, a picture of Christ’s love for his church (Ephesians 5:31–32). And the single life is honoured equally here, as a calling in which a person can serve God with undivided devotion (1 Corinthians 7:32–35). Leviticus 18:30; Ephesians 5:3–5 1 Thessalonians 4:3–8 1 Corinthians 7:1–9; Hebrews 13:4 Does God in this commandment forbid nothing more than adultery, and such like gross sins? Since our body and soul are both temples of the Holy Ghost, it is his will that we keep both pure and holy; for which reason he forbids all unchaste actions, gestures, words, thoughts, desires, and whatever may entice thereto. Since both our body and soul are temples of the Holy Spirit, he wants us to keep them both pure and holy. That is why he forbids all unchaste actions, gestures, words, thoughts, desires and whatever may lead us towards them. Jesus taught that lust in the heart is already adultery (Matthew 5:27–28), which shows that none of us is innocent here. But the motive the catechism gives is beautiful: our bodies are the dwelling place of God’s Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). Purity is not about shame but about honouring the God who lives in us, and his forgiveness reaches every failure. 1 Corinthians 15:33; Ephesians 5:18 Matthew 5:27–29; 1 Corinthians 6:18–20; Ephesians 5:3–4

Lord’s Day 42: The Eighth Commandment Part 3: Our Thankfulness The eighth commandment forbids not only crimes the courts would punish but every trick by which we take what belongs to others, including dishonest business, unfair prices and exploitation, as well as greed and waste. Positively, it calls us to seek our neighbour’s good, treat others as we would be treated, and work faithfully so that we can give to those in need. What does God forbid in the eighth commandment? Not only such theft and robbery as are punished by the magistrate, but God views as theft also all wicked tricks and devices whereby we seek to draw to ourselves our neighbor’s goods, whether by force or with show of right, such as unjust weights, ells, measures, wares, coins, usury, or any means forbidden of God; so, moreover, all covetousness, and all useless waste of his gifts. God forbids not only the theft and robbery that the government punishes. In his sight theft also includes all the cunning tricks and schemes by which we try to get our neighbour’s goods for ourselves, whether by force or by a show of legality, such as false weights, lengths and measures, poor goods, false money, extortionate interest, or any other means God has forbidden. He also forbids all greed and all wasteful misuse of his gifts. God cares about honest business, fair prices and just wages, the ordinary dealings of economic life (Proverbs 11:1). Theft can wear a suit as easily as a mask. And the root is greed, the restless sense that we do not have enough, which is answered only by knowing that in Christ we have everything we truly need (Hebrews 13:5). Exodus 22:1; 1 Corinthians 5:9–10; 6:9–10 Micah 6:9–11; Luke 3:14; James 5:1–6 Deuteronomy 25:13–16; Psalm 15:5; Proverbs 11:1; 12:22; Ezekiel 45:9–12; Luke 6:35 Luke 12:15; Ephesians 5:5 Proverbs 21:20; 23:20–21; Luke 16:10–13 But what does God require of thee in this commandment? That I further my neighbor’s good where I can and may, deal with him as I would have others deal with me, and labor faithfully that I may be able to help the poor in their need. That I do whatever I can and may for my neighbour’s good, that I treat him as I would like others to treat me, and that I work faithfully so that I may be able to help the poor in their need. The commandment against stealing becomes a call to generosity. Paul tells the thief not only to stop stealing but to work “so that he may have something to share with anyone in need” (Ephesians 4:28). Christ, who was rich, became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), and his people learn to hold their possessions with open hands. Isaiah 58:5–10; Matthew 7:12; Galatians 6:9–10 Ephesians 4:28

Lord’s Day 43: The Ninth Commandment Part 3: Our Thankfulness Words can wound or heal, destroy or build up. The ninth commandment forbids false testimony, twisting others’ words, gossip, slander and rash condemnation, and all lying and deceit, which the catechism calls the devil’s own work. Positively, it calls us to love the truth, speak it honestly and protect our neighbour’s good name. What is required in the ninth commandment? That I bear false witness against no one; wrest no one’s words; be no backbiter or slanderer; join in condemning no one unheard and rashly: but that I avoid, on pain of God’s heavy wrath, all lying and deceit, as being the proper works of the devil; in matters of judgment and justice, and in all other affairs, love, honestly speak and confess the truth; and, so far as I can, defend and promote my neighbor’s good name. That I never give false testimony against anyone, twist no one’s words, not gossip or slander, nor join in condemning anyone rashly or without a hearing. Rather, on pain of God’s heavy anger, I should avoid all lying and deceit as the devil’s own works. In court and everywhere else, I should love the truth, speak it honestly and confess it. And I should do what I can to defend and promote my neighbour’s honour and good name. The devil is “a liar and the father of lies” (John 8:44), and Jesus is “the truth” (John 14:6), so how we speak shows whose likeness we bear. This commandment searches our ordinary conversation: the half-truth, the unkind story, the quick assumption about someone’s motives. Love speaks the truth, and love also covers a neighbour’s faults rather than spreading them (1 Peter 4:8). Lord’s Day 44: The Tenth Commandment and the Use of the Law Part 3: Our Thankfulness The last commandment goes beneath all the others to the heart, forbidding even the smallest desire against God’s will. No one, not even the holiest believer, keeps the law perfectly in this life. Why then does God keep pressing it on us? So that we keep running to Christ for forgiveness, and keep asking the Spirit to make us more like him, until we are made perfect. What is required in the tenth commandment? That not even the least inclination or thought against any of God’s commandments ever enter into our heart; but that, with our whole heart, we continually hate all sin, and take pleasure in all righteousness. That not even the slightest desire or thought against any of God’s commandments should ever arise in our hearts. Rather, with all our hearts we should always hate all sin and take pleasure in all that is right. Coveting is the sin no one sees, and it was the commandment that finally showed Paul how sinful he was (Romans 7:7). It shows that God’s law is about the heart, not just behaviour. The answer to covetousness is contentment, and the secret of contentment is finding our treasure in Christ (Philippians 4:11–13). Psalm 19:7–14; 139:23–24; Romans 7:7–8 Can those who are converted to God keep these commandments perfectly? No; but even the holiest men, while in this life, have only a small beginning of this obedience, yet so that with earnest purpose they begin to live, not only according to some, but according to all the commandments of God. No. In this life even the holiest people have only a small beginning of this obedience. Nevertheless, with earnest purpose they begin to live not only according to some but according to all of God’s commandments. Honesty about our imperfection protects us from both pride and despair. We will never reach perfection in this life (1 John 1:8), but genuine believers truly begin to love all of God’s will, not just the parts that suit them. Real growth is often slow and small, and God delights in small beginnings. Ecclesiastes 7:20; Romans 7:14–15; 1 Corinthians 13:9; 1 John 1:8–10 Psalm 1:1–2; Romans 7:22–25; Philippians 3:12–16 Why, then, doth God so strictly enjoin upon us the ten commandments, since in this life no one can keep them? First, that all our life long we may learn more and more to know our sinful nature, and so the more earnestly seek forgiveness of sins and righteousness in Christ; secondly, that we may continually strive and beg from God the grace of the Holy Ghost, so as to become more and more changed into the image of God, till we attain finally to full perfection after this life. First, so that throughout our lives we may come to know our sinful nature better and better, and so more eagerly look to Christ for forgiveness of sins and righteousness. Second, so that we may never stop striving, and never stop praying to God for the grace of the Holy Spirit, to be renewed more and more into God’s image, until after this life we reach the goal of perfection. The law keeps doing two good things in the believer’s life. It keeps showing us our need, so that we keep running to Christ (Romans 7:24–25). And it shows us the shape of the life the Spirit is forming in us, so that we keep asking for his help. The goal is sure: one day “we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2). Psalm 32:5; Romans 3:19–26; 7:7, 24–25; 1 John 1:9 1 Corinthians 9:24; Philippians 3:12–14; 1 John 3:1–3

Lord’s Day 45: Prayer Part 3: Our Thankfulness The catechism ends with prayer, calling it the most important part of the thankfulness God asks of us. True prayer comes from the heart, is directed to the one true God, is humble about our need and confident in his promise to hear us for Christ’s sake. And Christ himself has given us a pattern: the Lord’s Prayer. Why is prayer necessary for Christians? Because it is the chief part of the thankfulness which God requires of us, and because God will give his grace and Holy Spirit only to such as earnestly and without ceasing beg them from him and render thanks unto him for them. Because prayer is the most important part of the thankfulness God requires of us. And also because God gives his grace and the Holy Spirit only to those who ask him for them sincerely and without ceasing, and who thank him for them. Prayer is gratitude in its most natural form: the child talking to the Father who has given everything. And God has chosen to give his best gifts in answer to prayer, as Jesus said: “how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:13). Prayer is not a technique for getting things but the life of a child with a Father. Psalm 50:14–15; 116:12–19; 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18 Matthew 7:7–8; Luke 11:9–13 What belongs to such prayer as God is pleased with and will hear? First, that from the heart we call only upon the one true God, who has revealed himself to us in his Word, for all that he has commanded us to ask of him; secondly, that we thoroughly know our need and misery, so as to humble ourselves before the face of his divine majesty; thirdly, that we be firmly assured that, notwithstanding our unworthiness, he will, for the sake of Christ our Lord, certainly hear our prayer, as he has promised us in his Word. First, that we call from the heart on the one true God only, who has revealed himself to us in his Word, for everything he has commanded us to ask. Second, that we thoroughly recognise our need and misery, so that we humble ourselves before his majesty. Third, that we rest on this firm foundation: that although we do not deserve it, God will certainly hear our prayer because of Christ our Lord, as he has promised us in his Word. Prayer rests not on our worthiness but on Christ’s. We come honestly, admitting our need, and boldly, trusting his promise (Hebrews 4:16). That combination of humility and confidence is only possible for people who know they are welcome because of someone else. Psalm 145:18–20; John 4:22–24; Romans 8:26–27; James 1:5; 1 John 5:14–15 2 Chronicles 7:14; Psalm 2:11; 34:18; 62:8; Isaiah 66:2; Revelation 4 Daniel 9:17–19; Matthew 7:8; John 14:13–14; 16:23; Romans 10:13; James 1:6 What has God commanded us to ask of him? All things necessary for soul and body, which Christ our Lord has comprised in the prayer taught us by himself. Everything we need, spiritually and physically, as embraced in the prayer Christ our Lord himself taught us. Nothing is too large or too small to bring to God. The Lord’s Prayer moves from God’s glory to our daily bread, from his kingdom to our sins and temptations (Matthew 6:9–13). It teaches us to want the right things in the right order, and it gives words to people who do not know how to pray. James 1:17; Matthew 6:33 What is the Lord’s Prayer? Our Father who art in heaven: Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen. Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory for ever. Amen. This prayer is short enough for a child and deep enough for a lifetime. It is the prayer of a family: “Our Father”, not my Father, so even alone we pray with the whole church. And every line is one that Jesus himself makes possible, by bringing us to the Father, bearing our debts and defeating the evil one. Matthew 6:9–13; Luke 11:2–4

Lord’s Day 46: Our Father in Heaven Part 3: Our Thankfulness The prayer begins by addressing God as Father, which awakens in us the childlike reverence and trust that are the foundation of all prayer. And he is our Father in heaven: not to suggest he is far away, but to lift our thoughts to his majesty, and to assure us that he has all power to give us what we need. Why has Christ commanded us to address God thus: Our Father? To awaken in us, at the very beginning of our prayer, that filial reverence and trust toward God which are to be the ground of our prayer; namely, that God has become our Father through Christ, and will much less deny us what we ask of him in faith than our parents refuse us earthly things. To awaken in us, at the very beginning of our prayer, the childlike reverence and trust in God that should be the foundation of our prayer: that God has become our Father through Christ, and will much less refuse us what we ask in faith than our earthly fathers refuse us earthly things. The first word sets the tone for everything. We are not petitioners before a reluctant king but children before a Father who loves to give (Matthew 7:9–11). That relationship was costly, for it was won by Christ, and so it is secure. Even when we pray badly, we pray as sons and daughters. Matthew 7:9–11; Luke 11:11–13 Why is it added: Who art in heaven? That we may have no earthly thought of the heavenly majesty of God, and may expect from his almighty power all things necessary for body and soul. So that we do not think of God’s heavenly majesty in an earthly way, and so that we expect from his almighty power everything we need for body and soul. In heaven reminds us of two things at once: God is far greater than we are, and he is able to do anything. A father who loves but cannot help, or who can help but does not love, would be a poor foundation. Our Father is both perfectly loving and almighty (Ephesians 3:20). Jeremiah 23:23–24; Acts 17:24–25 Matthew 6:25–34; Romans 8:31–32

Lord’s Day 47: The First Petition Part 3: Our Thankfulness The first petition asks that God’s name be honoured. We pray to know him truly and to praise him for his works, in which his power, wisdom, goodness, justice, mercy and truth shine out, and that our whole lives may bring honour rather than shame to his name. What is the first petition? Hallowed be thy name. That is: Enable us rightly to know thee, and to hallow, magnify, and praise thee in all thy works, in which shine forth thy power, wisdom, goodness, justice, mercy, and truth; and likewise so to order our whole life, in thought, word, and work, that thy name may not be blasphemed, but honored and praised on our account. Hallowed be your name. That is: help us first of all to know you rightly, and to honour, glorify and praise you in all your works, in which your almighty power, wisdom, goodness, justice, mercy and truth shine out. And help us also so to direct our whole lives, our thoughts, words and actions, that your name is never blasphemed because of us but always honoured and praised. Before we ask for anything for ourselves, Jesus teaches us to ask that God be seen and loved for who he is. This is the deepest desire of a heart changed by grace: not that we be admired, but that he be (Psalm 115:1). And it is a sobering prayer, because how we live either commends God’s name to others or brings it into disrepute. Jeremiah 9:23–24; 31:33–34; Matthew 16:17; John 17:3 Exodus 34:5–8; Psalm 145; Jeremiah 32:16–20; Luke 1:46–55, 68–75; Romans 11:33–36 Psalm 115:1; Matthew 5:16

Lord’s Day 48: The Second Petition Part 3: Our Thankfulness In praying for God’s kingdom we ask him to rule our own hearts by his Word and Spirit, to keep and grow his church, and to destroy the works of the devil and every power that rebels against him, until the day his kingdom comes in full and he is all in all. What is the second petition? Thy kingdom come. That is: So govern us by thy Word and Spirit that we may submit ourselves unto thee always more and more; preserve and increase thy Church; destroy the works of the devil, every power that exalteth itself against thee, and all wicked devices formed against thy holy Word, until the full coming of thy kingdom, wherein thou shalt be all in all. Your kingdom come. That is: so rule us by your Word and Spirit that more and more we submit to you. Keep your church and make it grow. Destroy the devil’s work, every power that rises up against you, and every wicked plan against your holy Word, until your kingdom comes in its fullness, in which you will be all in all. The kingdom of God is his loving rule, which began with Jesus and will one day fill the whole earth. To pray for it is to ask that it come first in our own hearts (Luke 17:21), then in the church and the world. It is a prayer of hope: whatever evil does now, the end of the story is that God will be “all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28). Psalm 119:5, 105; 143:10; Matthew 6:33 Psalm 122:6–9; Matthew 16:18; Acts 2:42–47 Romans 16:20; 1 John 3:8 Romans 8:22–23; Revelation 22:17, 20 1 Corinthians 15:28

Lord’s Day 49: The Third Petition Part 3: Our Thankfulness The third petition asks that we and all people would give up our own will and obey God’s will, which alone is good, without complaint, so that each of us might carry out our calling as gladly and faithfully as the angels in heaven. What is the third petition? Thy will be done in earth as it is in heaven. That is: Grant that we and all men may renounce our own will, and yield ourselves, without gainsaying, to thy will, which alone is good; that so every one may fulfill his office and calling as willingly and truly as the angels do in heaven. Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. That is: help us and all people to deny our own will and to obey your will, which alone is good, without any complaint. Help us each to carry out the work of our office and calling as willingly and faithfully as the angels in heaven. This is the prayer Jesus himself prayed in Gethsemane: “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). He surrendered his will for our sake, and because he did, we can trust that God’s will is good even when it is hard. And the catechism brings this into ordinary life: every honest job and calling can be done as service to God (Colossians 3:23). Matthew 7:21; 16:24–26; Luke 22:42; Romans 12:1–2; Titus 2:11–12 1 Corinthians 7:17–24; Ephesians 6:5–9 Psalm 103:20–21

Lord’s Day 50: The Fourth Petition Part 3: Our Thankfulness Asking for daily bread teaches us to depend on God for every ordinary need, and to see that he is the only source of all good. Without his blessing neither our work nor even his gifts would do us any good. So we learn to stop trusting in creatures and to rest our trust in him alone. What is the fourth petition? Give us this day our daily bread. That is: Be pleased to provide for all our bodily need, that we may thereby know that thou art the only fountain of all good, and that without thy blessing neither our care and labor nor thy gifts can profit us, and may therefore withdraw our trust from all creatures, and place it alone in thee. Give us this day our daily bread. That is: provide for all our physical needs, so that we may acknowledge that you are the only source of everything good, and that neither our care and work nor even your gifts can do us any good without your blessing. Help us therefore to withdraw our trust from all creatures and to put it in you alone. Most of us do not feel dependent on God for our food; it comes from the supermarket. This petition reminds us that every good thing is his gift (James 1:17), and that a full table without his blessing is still empty. It frees us from anxious striving and teaches the simple trust of a child who expects breakfast tomorrow (Matthew 6:31–33). Psalm 104:27–30; 145:15–16; Matthew 6:25–34 Acts 14:17; 17:25; James 1:17 Deuteronomy 8:3; Psalm 37:16; 127:1–2; 1 Corinthians 15:58 Psalm 55:22; 62; 146; Jeremiah 17:5–8; Hebrews 13:5–6

Lord’s Day 51: The Fifth Petition Part 3: Our Thankfulness We ask God, for the sake of Christ’s blood, not to hold against us our many sins or the evil that still clings to us. And we bring with the request a sign of his grace at work in us: our wholehearted intention to forgive our neighbour as we have been forgiven. What is the fifth petition? And forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors. That is: Be pleased, for the sake of Christ’s blood, not to impute to us, miserable sinners, our manifold transgressions, nor the evil which still always cleaves to us; as we also find this witness of thy grace in us, that it is our full purpose heartily to forgive our neighbor. And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. That is: for the sake of Christ’s blood, do not hold against us, poor sinners that we are, any of our sins or the evil that constantly clings to us, just as we too find this evidence of your grace in us, that we are fully determined wholeheartedly to forgive our neighbour. We need forgiveness every day, not only at conversion, and Christ’s blood is enough for every day (1 John 1:9). The link with forgiving others is not a bargain, as if we earned forgiveness by giving it, but a sign: forgiven people learn to forgive (Ephesians 4:32). When we struggle to forgive, the answer is to look again at how much we have been forgiven (Matthew 18:21–35). Psalm 51:1–7; 143:2; Romans 8:1; 1 John 2:1–2 Matthew 6:14–15; 18:21–35

Lord’s Day 52: The Sixth Petition and the Close of the Prayer Part 3: Our Thankfulness The catechism ends where the Christian life is still being fought: against the devil, the world and our own flesh. We ask God to hold us up by his Spirit until final victory. Then we close the prayer with praise, resting everything on God’s kingdom, power and glory, and say Amen: it is certain, because God hears us more surely than we feel our own desire. What is the sixth petition? And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. That is: Since we are so weak in ourselves that we can not stand a moment, while our deadly enemies—the devil, the world, and our own flesh—assail us without ceasing, be pleased to preserve and strengthen us by the power of thy Holy Spirit, that we may make firm stand against them, and not sink in this spiritual war, until we come off at last with complete victory. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. That is: by ourselves we are so weak that we cannot stand for a moment. And our sworn enemies, the devil, the world and our own flesh, never stop attacking us. So please uphold us and make us strong by the power of your Holy Spirit, so that we may stand firm against them and not be defeated in this spiritual war, until we finally win complete victory. Christians are not spiritual heroes but weak people kept by a strong God. We are in a real battle (Ephesians 6:10–13), and we cannot stand for a moment alone. But Christ has faced the tempter and won (Matthew 4:1–11), and he promises that God “will not let you be tempted beyond your ability” (1 Corinthians 10:13). The victory is sure because it is his. Psalm 103:14–16; John 15:1–5 2 Corinthians 11:14; Ephesians 6:10–13; 1 Peter 5:8 John 15:18–21 Romans 7:23; Galatians 5:17 Matthew 10:19–20; 26:41; Mark 13:33; Romans 5:3–5 1 Corinthians 10:13; 1 Thessalonians 3:13; 5:23 How do you close this Prayer? For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. That is: All this we ask of thee, because as our King, having power over all things, thou art both willing and able to give us all good, and that thereby not we but thy holy name may be glorified forever. For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory for ever. That is: we have made all these requests of you because, as our King with power over all things, you are both willing and able to give us all that is good; and because by this not we ourselves, but your holy name, should receive all the praise for ever. The prayer ends where all things will end, in the praise of God. We ask boldly because he is King and has all power, and we ask humbly because the glory belongs to him, not us (Romans 11:36). Even our requests become worship. Romans 10:11–13; 2 Peter 2:9 Psalm 115:1; John 14:13 What is the meaning of the word Amen? Amen means: So shall it truly and surely be. For my prayer is much more certainly heard of God than I feel in my heart that I desire these things of him. Amen means: this is sure to be! For my prayer is much more certainly heard by God than I feel in my heart that I desire these things from him. The catechism ends on a note of quiet confidence. Our feelings rise and fall, but God’s promises do not; he hears us more surely than we even feel our own longing. All the promises of God find their “Yes” in Christ, “That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory” (2 Corinthians 1:20). Isaiah 65:24; 2 Corinthians 1:20; 2 Timothy 2:13
